title: anomaly
text: anomaly detect baseline-window uint32 clear-consecutive uint8 cohort-prefix-len-v4 uint8 cohort-prefix-len-v6 uint8 confirm-duration uint16 corroboration-weight decimal-2 deviation-threshold decimal-2 enabled boolean min-cohort-size uint16 min-features-to-correlate uint8 observe incident-ring-size uint32 stale-incident-timeout uint32 shape action enumeration allowlist ip-prefix auto-revert-ttl uint16 blast-radius-cap uint16 kill-switch boolean limit-burst uint32 limit-rate uint64 limit-unit enumeration mode enumeration Behavioral anomaly detection and response subsystem. Two plugins fill this container. anomaly-detect owns the detect subtree and reports incidents on the event bus. anomaly-shape adds the shape subtree and acts on those incidents. Remove a plugin and its subtree disappears from the config. Report-only behavioral anomaly detector (emits incidents, takes no action). The detector reads one traffic-feature snapshot every second, and one second is one tick. It holds a baseline for each entity on three axes: the source address, the destination address, and the port. It publishes an incident on the event bus, and it writes no firewall rule. The shape subtree is what acts on an incident. Per-entity baseline horizon in ticks (the EWMA smoothing factor is derived from it). Ze derives the EWMA smoothing factor from this window: alpha is 2 divided by the window plus 1. The default 300 gives an alpha of 0.0066. A longer window makes the baseline slower and a short burst more visible. Ze folds a tick into the baseline only when the entity is not anomalous on that tick. A long anomaly cannot drift the baseline up to meet it. Consecutive below-threshold ticks before an active incident clears. One tick is one second. An active incident clears after this many ticks in a row below the threshold, and one tick above it resets the count to 0. The default 10 holds the incident for 10 seconds after the traffic stops. Source-prefix length that buckets IPv4 entities into peer-group cohorts. Ze masks the IPv4 address of the entity to this length and uses the result as the cohort key. Ze compares each entity against the other members of its cohort, which is how it scores rarity. A shorter length makes a larger cohort. min-cohort-size sets the smallest cohort Ze scores rarity in. Source-prefix length that buckets IPv6 entities into peer-group cohorts. Ze masks the IPv6 address of the entity to this length and uses the result as the cohort key. The default 48 groups a site together. Where the mask does not apply to the address, Ze falls back to the whole address. That entity then forms a cohort of one, and Ze scores it on its own baseline alone. Consecutive above-threshold ticks before an incident is confirmed and emitted. One tick is one second. Ze needs this many ticks in a row above the threshold, and one tick below it resets the count to 0. The default 3 delays an incident by 3 seconds and it drops a one-tick spike. Discount applied to a corroborating feature when Ze combines scores. Discount applied to corroborating features when combining scores. The discount stops correlated features from counting twice. Sigma at or above which a per-entity feature deviation fires. A feature fires when its z-score reaches this value. That score is the larger of two numbers. The first is the deviation from the entity own baseline. The second is the rarity of the value in the cohort of the entity. A lower value fires more features and raises the number of false incidents. The value also grades the severity Ze puts on an incident. Enable the behavioral anomaly detector (report-only; emits incidents, takes no action). The default false leaves the detector idle: it starts no ticker and it holds no baseline. Set it true and Ze attaches to the traffic-feature service and starts the one-second ticker. An entity needs 3 ticks of samples before Ze scores its deviation from its own baseline. Minimum members in a cohort before Ze scores peer-group rarity. Minimum cohort members before peer-group rarity is scored. A cohort is a source-prefix bucket. A smaller cohort uses self-deviation only. Minimum distinct features that must fire before Ze scores an incident. Minimum distinct features that must fire on one entity and one window before Ze scores an incident. The minimum correlates weak signals, so one feature alone raises no incident. Incident lifecycle store for confirmed anomaly incidents. The store keeps each confirmed incident from its start to its end. `show anomaly observe` reads the store, so it can report the duration of a finished incident. Maximum number of incidents the ring keeps in memory. When the ring is full, the oldest finalized incident is dropped first. Seconds before an open incident with no clear event is finalized. The detector stops reporting an entity that goes idle, and it sends no clear event for that entity. This timeout is the limit on how long such an incident reads as active. Autonomous responder: shadow (log-only) or armed (live per-source firewall actions). The responder reads the incidents the detect subtree publishes, and it acts on a source incident alone. In armed mode it writes an nftables table named ze_anomaly-shape, with one term for each armed source. The chain of that table attaches to the input hook at priority -200, so it acts on the traffic addressed to this host. Armed action: rate-limit the source (surgical) or drop it (fallback). limit writes an nftables counter and a rate limit on the source prefix, and it reads limit-rate, limit-unit and limit-burst. drop writes a counter and discards every packet from that source. Ze applies the action to each armed source, and it applies nothing while mode is shadow. Protected source prefixes that ze never arms an action against. The list guards against self-lockout, for management sources and control-plane sources. Seconds after the last signal before an armed action reverts by itself. This ceiling holds whether or not a clear event arrives, so an armed action can never stay in place indefinitely. Maximum concurrently-armed live actions; further arm attempts are refused. Ze counts the sources that carry a live action. At this cap Ze refuses to arm one more source, writes a warning, and raises the arm-refused metric. A source that is armed already costs the count nothing, because that path only refreshes its auto-revert-ttl. The cap bounds the firewall table an incident storm can produce. When true, revert every armed action and force the responder to shadow. Ze runs the revert when it reads the config, so it also removes what an earlier instance of the responder left in the firewall. The responder then answers every incident as shadow does, and it writes a log line in place of a rule. Set the leaf back to false to let the responder arm again. Burst allowance for the limit action. The burst is the number of packets Ze lets through above the rate before it starts to drop. The default 0 gives no allowance, so the rate applies from the first packet. Ze gives the value to the nftables limit expression. The leaf changes nothing while the action is drop. Rate for the limit action, in packets per limit-unit. The rate counts packets, and limit-unit gives the time. The default 1000, with the default unit second, lets 1000 packets a second through from each armed source. A value of 0 is refused at commit while the action is limit. The leaf changes nothing while the action is drop. Time unit for limit-rate. The unit divides limit-rate. A rate of 1000 with the unit minute lets 1000 packets a minute through. Ze gives the word to the nftables limit expression, and a word outside the four is refused at commit. The leaf changes nothing while the action is drop. Responder mode: shadow or armed. shadow, the default, logs the action it would take and installs nothing. armed installs live per-source firewall actions.

title: bfd
text: bfd bind-v6 boolean enabled boolean multi-hop-session <peer local vrf> local string min-ttl uint8 peer string profile string shutdown boolean vrf string persist-dir string profile <name> auth key-id uint8 secret string type enumeration desired-min-tx-us uint32 detect-multiplier uint8 echo desired-min-echo-tx-us uint32 passive boolean required-min-rx-us uint32 single-hop-session <peer vrf interface> interface string local string peer string profile string shutdown boolean vrf string BFD control configuration for Ze. The container holds the plugin switch, the reusable profiles, and the sessions an operator pins. A session that BGP or a static route asks for at runtime does not appear here. A protocol client reaches the plugin through its Service interface instead. Bind an IPv6 socket beside the IPv4 socket on every loop. When this leaf is true, the BFD plugin also binds an IPv6 socket (::0) alongside the IPv4 socket for every (vrf, mode) loop. The paired sockets share the same RX channel through a transport.Dual wrapper, and send routes by destination address family. Stage 2b (spec-bfd-2b-ipv6-transport) ships this leaf. A pinned IPv6 session requires the leaf to be set explicitly, so an operator who does not need IPv6 does not open a second socket per loop. Master switch for the BFD plugin. The default is true. false stops every BFD session, the ones pinned in this bfd container and the ones a protocol client asks for at runtime. A reload to false stops the pinned sessions already running. A BGP peer that carries a bfd container gets a refusal instead of a session, so a peer in strict mode stays down and a peer outside strict mode runs without BFD. To stop the session of one peer only, remove the bfd container from that peer or set its enabled leaf to false. Multi-hop BFD session (RFC 5883). Port 4784, no GTSM. The 255-TTL test of a single-hop session cannot work over several hops. The min-ttl leaf is the cheap protection here, and authentication is the strong one. Ze refuses an entry whose profile enables echo. RFC 5883 Section 3 states that the Echo function MUST NOT be used over multiple hops. The local leaf is required here, and it is optional on a single-hop session. Local source address. Required for multi-hop. Ze refuses an entry that omits this leaf. The address is the source of every Control packet Ze sends, and it is part of the session key. RFC 5883 Section 4.1 states that two sessions between the same pair of systems must differ in at least one endpoint address. The reason is that the first packet carries a Your Discriminator of 0. Minimum acceptable TTL on receive. Weak replacement for GTSM on multi-hop paths. Ze discards a Control packet whose TTL is less than this value, and the test is inclusive, so a TTL equal to it passes. A peer sends with a TTL of 255, so 254 allows one router between the peer and Ze. Raise the value toward 255 when the peer is fewer hops away, because a higher floor rejects a packet sent from further away. Address of the remote system this session runs to. The value is the first word after the list name, so multi-hop-session 203.0.113.9 names this peer. Ze refuses an address it cannot parse, and IPv4 and IPv6 are both accepted. The peer, the local address and the VRF together identify the session. Name of the timer profile this session takes its intervals from. Ze refuses a name that no profile declares, and it refuses a profile that enables echo. Without this leaf the session takes the engine values: a detect multiplier of 3, and 1000000 microseconds for both the transmit target and the receive floor. Hold the session administratively down and keep its configuration. The session stays configured and stops sending control packets, so a peer sees it go down. Delete the list entry to remove it instead. Routing instance the session runs in. The default instance is named default. A name other than default binds the socket to the VRF device of that name. Ze runs one socket for each pair of VRF and hop mode, so every multi-hop session in one VRF shares it. An empty value is read as default. DEPRECATED. A non-empty value opts a session into sequence persistence. DEPRECATED, retained for back-compat and scheduled for removal. The value is no longer interpreted as a directory. TX sequence numbers for Meticulous Keyed authentication now persist to the shared managed store (the database/ tree), instead of a loose file. A non-empty value still opts a session into persistence. RFC 5880 Section 6.7.3 requires the sequence to survive process restarts. Without this leaf set, Meticulous sessions still work at runtime, but a fresh process loses its sequence floor until the peer's replay window slides forward. Reusable timer and feature profile. Reusable timer and feature profile. Sessions reference a profile by name and inherit every field below. Authentication parameters (RFC 5880 Section 6.7). RFC 5880 Section 6.7 authentication parameters. Sessions inheriting this profile sign every outgoing Control packet with the configured type, and verify incoming packets with the same key. There is no default type, and authentication runs only on the type the operator names here. Auth Key ID (RFC 5880 Section 6.7.1). Ze writes the value into the authentication section of every Control packet it sends. Ze discards a received packet that carries another value, which RFC 5880 Section 6.7.2 requires for Simple Password. Both ends must name the same key-id and the same secret. The range is 0 to 255. Shared secret, redacted from `ze config show` output. Shared secret. Redacted from `ze config show` output. The MD5 variants take a secret of up to 16 bytes (RFC 5880 Section 6.7.3) and the SHA1 variants one of up to 20 bytes (Section 6.7.4). Both pad a shorter secret with zeros, and a longer one is refused at parse time. The simple-password type carries the secret itself on the wire, so it must be 1 to 16 bytes, and a longer one is refused at parse time too (RFC 5880 Section 6.7.2). Authentication type, which the operator must name. Authentication type. There is no default. The operator names the type, and simple-password is never selected on their behalf. simple-password is RFC 5880 Section 6.7.2 Simple Password. The password travels in clear in every Control packet and the section never changes, so it protects against a misconfigured peer and against nothing else. It does not protect against a listener on the path, who reads the password from one packet, and it carries no Sequence Number, so a captured packet can be replayed. Choose a keyed type wherever the path is not already trusted. Local target transmit rate in microseconds. Local target transmit rate in microseconds. The slow-start floor of 1 000 000 us applies while the session is not Up, per RFC 5880 Section 6.8.3. Consecutive missed Control packets that trigger a Down transition. Number of consecutive missed Control packets that trigger a Down transition. RFC 5880 Section 6.8.4. BFD Echo mode (RFC 5880 Section 6.4, RFC 5881 Section 5). RFC 5880 Section 6.4 / RFC 5881 Section 5 Echo mode. Echo mode is single-hop only, because RFC 5883 Section 3 prohibits multi-hop echo: a multi-hop session or BGP peer that uses an echo profile is refused. When echo is active, the engine sends echo packets on UDP port 3785 at the peer's advertised RequiredMinEchoRxInterval. The engine then slows its async Control TX to the peer's RequiredMinRxInterval. Local target echo transmit rate in microseconds. Local target echo transmit rate in microseconds. The effective echo rate is max(local desired, peer RequiredMinEchoRx). Wait for a peer Control packet before this session transmits. Active, which is the default, transmits from session creation. Passive transmits nothing until a Control packet arrives from the peer. RFC 5883 Section 4.3. A single-hop session, BGP peer or static next-hop that uses a passive profile is refused: RFC 5881 Section 3 requires the Active role on a single hop. Minimum inter-packet gap the local end can handle, in microseconds. Ze advertises the value as Required Min RX Interval, and a peer that obeys it does not transmit faster. The detection time is the peer's Detect Multiplier times the larger of this value and the peer's Desired Min TX Interval. While echo mode runs, Ze raises the advertised value to 1000000 microseconds and starts a Poll sequence, because the echo packets already prove the path. Per-link BFD session on port 3784 with TTL 255 (RFC 5881). Per-link BFD session (RFC 5881). Port 3784, TTL=255. A protocol client MUST NOT use this list. A protocol client calls the plugin Service interface at runtime. Egress interface name. Ze binds the socket of the loop to this interface with SO_BINDTODEVICE. One socket serves every session of one VRF and hop mode. Ze binds it only when each session in the default VRF names the same interface. A mix of names leaves the socket unbound, with a warning in the log. In a VRF other than default the VRF device wins, and this leaf is dropped. Local source address (optional). While the leaf is absent, the kernel selects the source address. The address is part of the session key. A change to it therefore releases the running session, and creates a new one at the next config load. Peer IPv4 or IPv6 address. The value is the first word after the list name, so single-hop-session 203.0.113.9 names this peer. Ze refuses an address it cannot parse, and IPv4 and IPv6 are both accepted. RFC 5881 Section 5 requires a received TTL of 255, so Ze discards a Control packet from this peer that crossed a router. Named profile to inherit timer parameters from. Ze refuses a name that no profile declares. Without this leaf the session takes the engine values: a detect multiplier of 3, and 1000000 microseconds for both the transmit target and the receive floor. When true, the session stays in AdminDown state. RFC 5880 Section 6.8.16. The session keeps its configuration and its place in the list, and Ze holds it in AdminDown. Ze applies the value again at each reload, so a change from true to false brings the session back with no restart. Delete the list entry to remove the session instead. Routing instance the session runs in. The default instance is named default. A name other than default binds the socket to the VRF device of that name. The interface leaf of every session in that VRF is then dropped, and Ze logs the names it dropped once for each loop. An empty value is read as default.

title: bgp-epe
text: bgp-epe peer <address> sid-index uint32 weight uint8 srgb lower-bound uint32 upper-bound uint32 Instantiate BGP Egress Peer Engineering segments. The internal bgp-epe plugin consumes state events from attached BGP sessions. Each configured peer gets a persistent PeerNode SID index. While its session is established, the corresponding local label is popped and forwarded to the peer by the selected MPLS FIB writer. State withdrawal removes that label and its BGP-LS advertisement. Configure bgp-ls-export to advertise the native state to collectors. This SRGB must be reserved exclusively for these EPE labels and must not overlap another label producer. BGP session whose connected peer is an EPE next hop. Assign one distinct SRGB index to each established session's remote peer. Removing an assignment removes its forwarding label and withdraws its native BGP-LS state. Persistent PeerNode SID index in the EPE SRGB. Unique offset into the configured SRGB. The assignment remains stable across process restart and session flap. PeerNode SID load-balancing weight. Relative load-balancing weight advertised in the PeerNode SID attribute. Reserve the local label range for EPE PeerNode segments. Local SRGB reserved for EPE PeerNode segments. First label in the EPE SRGB. Inclusive lower label bound; labels below 16 are reserved by MPLS. Last label in the EPE SRGB. Inclusive upper label bound, which must be at least the lower bound.

title: bgp-ls-export
text: bgp-ls-export domain <name> instance-id uint64 native-area uint32 native-instance uint64 protocol-id uint8 source string Export native routing state through BGP-LS. Export the running native IGP databases to BGP peers that attach this internal plugin with state/refresh receive and update send grants. Each database snapshot replaces prior node, link, prefix, and SRv6 SID advertisements. Removed identities are withdrawn before replacements. The exporter retains at most 65536 routes and refuses a replacement exceeding that bound without changing the last accepted database. This feature requires the in-process engine event bus; it does not originate from a forked plugin. Set the 64-bit BGP-LS Instance-ID of a native domain. Assign a routing-universe Instance-ID to one native domain. Unmapped domains retain the source's native identifier. Eight-octet routing-universe identifier. Full-width Instance-ID placed in originated NLRIs for the selected domain. Numeric source area or IS-IS level. Native numeric OSPF area or IS-IS level published by the source. Source instance identifier. Native instance number published by the selected routing protocol. BGP-LS source Protocol-ID. Protocol identifier of the native snapshot selected by this mapping. Native source namespace. Registered link-state publisher namespace, such as isis, ospf, or bgp-epe.

title: class-of-service
text: class-of-service ieee-802.1p <name> egress priority <value> pcp uint8 ingress pcp <value> priority uint8 Named class-of-service profiles. A profile maps the 3-bit PCP field of an 802.1Q header to an internal priority, in the ingress direction and in the egress direction. An interface leaf and a unit leaf name the profile they use. An 802.1p QoS profile. The profile defines the mapping between the 3-bit PCP field in the 802.1Q header and the internal priorities. It covers the ingress direction and the egress direction. Priority-to-PCP mapping of a transmitted tagged frame. Ze reads this mapping when it stamps the PCP field of a frame it transmits. Map one internal priority to a transmitted PCP value. The list key is the internal priority, so the list holds at most one entry for each of the eight priorities. PCP value Ze stamps in the 802.1Q header. IEEE 802.1Q defines the Priority Code Point field, which is 3 bits wide and holds a value from 0 to 7. PCP-to-priority mapping of a received tagged frame. Ze reads this mapping when it takes the internal priority of a frame it receives. Map one received PCP value to an internal priority. The list key is the PCP value, so the list holds at most one entry for each of the eight values. Internal priority Ze gives to a matching frame. The value runs from 0 to 7.

title: connected
text: connected Connected route redistribution. Presence enables the plugin. The container carries no leaf, so writing it is the whole configuration. The plugin watches each interface address event and emits the network prefix of that address on the redistribute event bus. It counts the addresses of one prefix, so two addresses in one subnet announce the prefix once. The withdrawal waits for the last address of that prefix. The plugin registers the connected route source, and a redistribute statement names that source.

title: control-plane-protection
text: control-plane-protection bgp burst uint32 over-limit-policy enumeration protected-port uint16 rate rate-spec trusted-source string Control-plane policing configuration. Ze compiles the containers under it into one nftables table named ze_copp, which carries a base input chain at priority 0. The ze_ prefix is what makes the firewall backend own that table and withdraw it when you delete the configuration. The bgp container is the only policy Ze builds today. Rate-limit new TCP connections to the BGP listen port. The container carries presence, so Ze builds the ze_copp table when you write it and removes the table when you delete it. The chain accepts an established or related connection first, then a connection from each trusted-source prefix, and applies the rate to what is left. Burst size (packets or bytes matching the rate unit). The unit follows the unit of rate: a packet count where rate counts packets, and a byte count where rate names a byte unit. The leaf has no default, and Ze gives the kernel a burst of 0 when it is absent. What Ze does with the packets that exceed the rate limit. accept, the default, counts the over-limit packets and lets them through. The limit then reports load and stops nothing. drop discards a new TCP connection to a protected port once the rate is exceeded. Either setting reaches the over-limit packets alone. The input chain keeps an accept policy, so SSH, ICMP and every service this table never names stay reachable. The first term accepts an established session before the limit is read, so drop never closes a session that is already up. TCP port(s) the control-plane policing rules protect, 179 (BGP) by default. TCP port(s) to protect. Ze uses 179, the BGP port, when this leaf is omitted. Set a different value when the BGP listener uses another port. Rate limit for new connections (e.g., 100/second). The leaf is mandatory, so Ze refuses the container without it. The value is a count, an optional byte unit, and a time unit, as in 100/second or 1mbytes/second. The limit reaches a new TCP connection to a protected port alone, because the chain accepts an established connection before it. Source prefixes that bypass the rate limit. Typically the addresses of configured BGP peers. Ze adds one accept term for each prefix, above the rate limit term. The term matches TCP from that source to a protected port, so a trusted peer never meets the limit. Ze refuses a value that is not an IPv4 prefix or an IPv6 prefix.

title: ddos
text: ddos detect absolute-floor uint32 baseline-window uint32 bps-floor uint64 bps-threshold-multiplier decimal-2 bps-trigger-enable boolean characterize-enable boolean characterize-timeout uint16 characterize-window uint16 check-interval uint16 clear-consecutive-checks uint16 confirm-duration uint16 enabled boolean entropy-threshold decimal-2 policy default-action enumeration rule <prefix> action enumeration match enumeration scope enumeration startup-grace uint16 threshold-multiplier decimal-2 top-n-sources uint16 flowspec action enumeration announce-rate-limit uint16 backoff-cap uint32 blackhole-fallback boolean confidence-min uint8 hold-down uint32 max-mitigation-duration uint32 probe-interval uint16 probe-rate uint32 probe-window uint16 rate-limit-bytes uint64 response-level enumeration flowtriq api-base string api-key string enabled boolean node-uuid string local confidence-min uint8 forward-mitigation boolean max-mitigation-duration uint32 response-level enumeration observe incident-ring-size uint32 stale-incident-timeout uint32 Distributed denial-of-service detection and mitigation subsystem. Distributed denial-of-service detection and mitigation subsystem. This module declares the container, and the flowtriq, observe, local and flowspec plugins each augment it. The detect subtree decides that an attack is present, and a responder under one of those subtrees acts on the event. Detect a volumetric attack from the traffic Ze already sees. Detection is separate from mitigation: this container decides that an attack is happening and emits an event. A responder under flowspec or local is what acts on that event, and none is armed by default. Minimum threshold in PPS regardless of baseline. Minimum threshold in PPS regardless of baseline, default 5000. A quiet link cannot trigger on a small burst, because the threshold never falls under this value. Five times this value is also the packet-rate escape from startup-grace, so a rate over 25000 PPS triggers at the default while the grace period runs. Rolling baseline window size in samples. Rolling baseline window size in samples, and one sample is one evaluation, so one check-interval. The window p99 is recalculated every 10 admitted samples, so a cold detector runs on absolute-floor alone for its first 10 evaluations. A sample taken while the rate is over the threshold is refused, so an attack cannot raise the threshold that detects it. One sample in 3600 consecutive refused samples is admitted, which lets a lasting rise in traffic move the baseline. A persisted baseline is restored only when it carries 50 samples or more. Minimum bandwidth in bits/sec below which the BPS trigger is inert. Minimum bandwidth in bits/sec below which the BPS trigger is inert. The default is 50 Mbps. The value is expressed in bits/sec, which is the operator unit. The detector's internal rate is bytes/sec, and it converts the value. Baseline p99 multiplier for the bandwidth (BPS) trigger. Baseline p99 multiplier for the bandwidth (BPS) trigger. The trigger catches low-PPS, high-bandwidth amplification, such as NTP, memcached and CLDAP, that the packet-rate threshold misses. Enable the bandwidth (BPS) trigger beside the PPS threshold. Enable the bandwidth (BPS) trigger alongside the PPS threshold. When this leaf is false, only the packet-rate threshold can trigger detection. Run Stage-2 flow characterization on a detected attack. Run Stage-2 flow characterization. The stage classifies the family and the narrowest vector from the flow-export recent-flow ring, and emits AttackCharacterized. When this leaf is false, the detector still emits the coarse AttackDetected target from traffic-usage. Milliseconds budget for the on-trigger queries. Milliseconds budget for the on-trigger traffic-usage and flow-recent queries. On timeout, the detector falls back to the best available target. Seconds of recent flows to consider when characterizing an attack. Seconds of recent flows to consider when characterizing. Flows last seen before this window are ignored. Flows with no timestamp are always kept. Seconds between detection evaluations. Seconds between detection evaluations. Both rate feeds publish once a second: the traffic-statistics service, and the interface rate collector Ze falls back to when that service is absent. The detector folds this many samples and evaluates their PEAK, so a flood shorter than the interval still reaches the threshold. Every leaf that counts ticks against the threshold counts evaluations, so its wall-clock meaning is multiplied by this value. The default 1 evaluates every second. Consecutive evaluations below threshold before clearing. The count of consecutive evaluations under the threshold that ends an attack. The first one under the threshold moves an active detector to the clearing state and counts as the first check. The default 10 therefore holds the attack live for ten evaluations, which is ten seconds at the default check-interval. One evaluation back over the threshold returns the detector to active and drops the count. Consecutive evaluations above threshold before triggering. The count of consecutive evaluations over the threshold that arms the detector. One evaluation is check-interval seconds, one second at the default. The default 3 needs three unbroken evaluations over the threshold. A value of 0 or 1 triggers on the first one. One evaluation back under the threshold returns the detector to idle and restarts the count. Enable the DDoS detector. Enable the DDoS detector. Left false, the detector subscribes to no rate feed, so it takes no sample and its baseline stays cold. A commit rebuilds the detector and restores the persisted baseline either way, and the subscription is what this leaf controls. Source-address Shannon entropy in bits that marks an attack distributed. Source-address Shannon entropy (bits) at or above which an attack is logged as distributed or spoofed. A value of 0 is a single source, and a higher value is more sources. Allow and deny traffic policy applied to a detected attack. Allow/deny traffic policy applied to detected attacks, indexed by prefix. Ze evaluates the policy by longest-prefix match, where the most specific rule wins, and not by config order. The policy replaces the removed per-responder allowlists. The detector enforces it once and encodes the exempt or mitigate decision on the emitted event, so the responders obey it with no config read. Disposition when no rule matches the attack. Disposition when no rule matches. deny means defend, which is detection plus mitigation. allow means exempt from detection entirely. One allow or deny rule matched against an attack, keyed by prefix. One allow/deny rule matched against an attack, keyed by prefix. Precedence is longest-prefix match, so a /24 rule beats a covering /16 with no ordering. allow exempts matching traffic and deny subjects it to DDoS handling. allow exempts the matched traffic and deny subjects it to DDoS handling. The scope leaf decides how far each one reaches. allow at mitigation scope records the incident and installs no block, and allow at detection scope suppresses the incident. deny at detection scope also records without a block, and deny at mitigation scope is full handling. Whether the prefix matches the attack source, the destination, or either. Whether the prefix matches the attack source, the victim destination, or either. A source rule takes effect once the attack sources are characterized. Stage the action governs, mitigation or detection. Stage the action governs. mitigation means detect and record, and for allow it does not block. detection means that for allow the incident is suppressed entirely. Seconds after startup where only extreme spikes trigger. Seconds after startup where only extreme spikes trigger, default 90. The count follows the rate feed, one per second, so check-interval does not change it. A cold baseline warms during the grace period, and the grace stops that warm-up from firing on itself. Two things still trigger: a packet rate over five times absolute-floor, and the bandwidth trigger once its own baseline is ready. Baseline p99 multiplier for the dynamic threshold. Baseline p99 multiplier for the dynamic threshold. The threshold is the larger of two numbers: the window p99 multiplied by this leaf, and absolute-floor. The default 3.00 therefore triggers at three times the p99 of normal traffic. A changed value reaches the threshold at the next recalculation, which is within 10 admitted samples. Maximum number of attacker source addresses ranked into TopSources by packet volume. Maximum number of attacker source addresses ranked into TopSources by packet volume, default 10. Ties are broken by address. The same ranked list is what a source-matching policy rule reads, and every address in it has to fall inside the rule prefix before that rule matches. Answer a detected attack by announcing a BGP FlowSpec rule. The rule is announced to a peer, so the traffic is dropped upstream and never reaches this router. It needs a peer that accepts FlowSpec, which is what separates it from the local responder. FlowSpec traffic-action: discard or rate-limit. Mandatory, with no default. Neither discard nor rate-limit is universally safe, so this leaf has no default. discard announces an RFC 8955 traffic-rate of 0, which drops the characterized attack flow. rate-limit announces a byte rate, and it requires an explicit rate-limit-bytes. A rate-limit-bytes of 0 is a valid choice, and it is equivalent to discard on the wire. Maximum FlowSpec announcements per minute. The most FlowSpec announcements Ze sends in any 60 second window. An announcement over the limit is refused and logged, and the responder stays idle, so the next attack characterization inside the window announces nothing upstream and the one after the window rolls does. The limit protects the BGP sessions the rule goes to: a peer that drops the session over announce churn loses every rule it holds. 10 is the default, and the range is 1 to 600. Maximum hold-down after exponential backoff. Each probe that saturates doubles the current hold-down, and this value stops the doubling. Ze refuses a backoff-cap under hold-down, and the upper bound is 604800 seconds. 3600 is the default, which stops the wait at one hour. Announce an immediate upstream discard on a critical-severity AttackDetected. When true, a critical-severity AttackDetected (a peak of 5x the threshold or more) engages an immediate upstream discard, in the style of RTBH, and it does not wait for characterization. When false, the default, ze announces the upstream rule only from AttackCharacterized. The rule is then precise before the box goes blind behind the filter. Minimum incident confidence (0-100) to announce an upstream rule from a characterized attack. The default is 0, which accepts any confidence. The blackhole-fallback fast path never applies this minimum, because AttackDetected carries no confidence. Minimum seconds before the first leak-probe after announcement. The responder counts one second for each AttackOngoing event the detector emits, and the detector emits one for each traffic sample. The rule stays at full strength for this long, and the first leak-probe follows. A probe that saturates doubles the wait, up to backoff-cap. The range is 1 to 86400 seconds, and 300 is the default. Maximum seconds a FlowSpec rule stays announced (0 = no cap). The responder measures this against the wall clock, and not against the probe. An attack that goes quiet stops the AttackOngoing events the probe counts, which is the case the probe cannot see. 0 removes the cap, so the rule then stays until a probe withdraws it. 3600 is the default, and the range is 0 to 604800 seconds. Seconds between leak-probe attempts after hold-down. After the hold-down ends the responder waits this long. It then narrows the rule to probe-rate and watches what arrives. 60 is the default, and the range is 1 to 3600

enabled boolean insecure boolean server <name> ip ip-address port listener-port ui-mode enumeration Environment settings for API transports The api-server container under it is the shared parent of the REST and gRPC transports. ze-rest-conf and ze-grpc-conf merge their rest and grpc containers into it, so a transport compiled out leaves no container to configure. API engine settings (shared parent for the REST/gRPC transports) The token leaf here is shared by both transports. Each transport starts only when its own enabled leaf is true, or when ze.api-server.rest.enabled or ze.api-server.grpc.enabled starts it. Ze parses the addresses, the CORS origin and the TLS pair even when the transport stays off. gRPC API transport. Authenticated non-loopback listeners require tls-cert and tls-key. A listen address that is not loopback must carry authentication and TLS, and Ze refuses to start the server without them. Without TLS the bearer token that gates each call crosses the network in clear. Ze accepts TLS 1.2 as its lowest version. Enable gRPC API server The default is false, so config starts no gRPC listener until the leaf is true. The environment variable ze.api-server.grpc.enabled starts the transport with no leaf written. Ze parses the addresses and the TLS pair even when the transport stays off. gRPC API listen endpoints The ze:listener extension marks this list, so config validation collects each endpoint and refuses a second listener that binds the same protocol, port and address. An empty list still binds one endpoint, 0.0.0.0 port 50051, from the refine defaults under it. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and an IPv4 address never overlaps an IPv6 address. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. Path to TLS certificate file for gRPC Write tls-cert and tls-key together. Ze refuses to start the server when one of the two is written and the other is not. Ze reads the pair from disk at start, so a path that names no file stops the server with an error. Path to TLS private key file for gRPC The leaf names the file that holds the private key of tls-cert, and Ze reads the two together at start. Ze marks the leaf ze:sensitive, so ze config dump prints the value $9$-encoded. REST and HTTP transport for the API server. A plain HTTP listener is restricted to loopback. To reach the API from another host, put a TLS terminator in front of the listener. CORS allowed origin (empty disables CORS headers) Ze copies the value into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header of each API answer, and validates nothing in it. An empty leaf sends no CORS header, and a preflight request then gets 204 with no header. A preflight answer permits GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS, permits the Authorization and Content-Type headers, and holds for 86400 seconds. Enable REST API server The default is false, so config starts no REST listener until the leaf is true. The environment variable ze.api-server.rest.enabled starts the transport with no leaf written. Ze parses the addresses and the CORS origin even when the transport stays off. REST API listen endpoints The ze:listener extension marks this list, so config validation collects each endpoint and refuses a second listener that binds the same protocol, port and address. An empty list still binds one endpoint, 0.0.0.0 port 8081, from the refine defaults under it. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and an IPv4 address never overlaps an IPv6 address. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. Bearer token for API authentication. When the token is set, a client MUST send the header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. Leave the leaf empty to allow unauthenticated access. BGP protocol environment settings, applied before any peer-level config. The container controls the OPEN wait timeout and the initial announce delay. Delay between reactor Ready and first UPDATE (duration, 0s-1h) The environment variable ze.bgp.announce.delay overrides the leaf. Ze holds every peer start for the delay after the reactor is otherwise Ready, which staggers route emission over a restart. Seconds to wait for peer OPEN after TCP connect The environment variable ze.bgp.openwait overrides the leaf. Ze arms the hold timer with the value after it sends OPEN. Ze resets that timer to the negotiated hold time when the peer OPEN arrives. BMP receiver settings The receiver starts only when enabled is true and the server list holds one entry at least. Ze stores each Route Monitoring message it accepts in the BMP RIB, and show bmp rib reads that RIB. Enable BMP receiver The default is false. The receiver needs this leaf true and one server entry at least, so enabled true on its own binds no address. Maximum concurrent BMP sessions The default is 100 and the range is 1 to 1000. The count is per listener, so two server entries admit twice this number of sessions. Over the limit Ze closes the new connection and logs a warning, and the sessions already open keep running. Action for received BMP Route Monitoring messages monitor is the default and is the only action Ze performs. redistribute is accepted by the schema and is not implemented: Ze writes a warning in the log and acts as monitor. Under monitor the routes of a BMP Route Monitoring message go to the BMP RIB, which show bmp rib reads. They reach neither BGP best-path selection nor the FIB. BMP receiver listen endpoints The ze:listener extension marks this list, so config validation refuses a second listener that binds the same protocol, port and address. Ze opens one TCP listener for each entry. A bind that fails is logged, and the other entries keep their listener. An empty list binds nothing, because the receiver has no default endpoint. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and an IPv4 address never overlaps an IPv6 address. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. Chaos fault injection settings Ze wraps the clock, the dialer and the listener factory with a fault injector while seed is not 0. The block exists to test Ze against slow timers and failed connections. A production config leaves the block out. Fault probability per operation (0.0-1.0) 0.1 injects a fault into one operation in ten. Ze uses 0.1 for a value that is not a number, and for a value outside 0.0 to 1.0. The leaf does nothing while seed is 0. PRNG seed (0 = disabled) Ze builds the fault injector only while the seed is not 0. The same seed replays the same sequence of faults, so a failed run can be repeated. A seed of -1 takes the seed from the clock, and Ze logs the value it took. Ze applies the ze command line after the config load, so a seed given there replaces the seed in this leaf. CLI session settings The container holds the default output format and the transcript switch. Both leaves apply to every CLI session this daemon serves. Default output format settings The container holds the default leaf alone. A session overrides it with set cli format, which changes that one session and no other. Default output format when no pipe operator is specified text writes space-aligned columns, table draws a box around them, json pretty-prints, yaml writes YAML, and ndjson writes one JSON object on each line. A format operator on the command line, such as | json, wins over this leaf, and so does set cli format. Ze falls back to text for a value it does not know. CLI session transcript recording to $XDG_DATA_HOME/ze/transcripts/ enabled writes one file for each session, named transcript-DATE-TIME-PID.log, with mode 0600 in a directory with mode 0700. Each entry holds the time, the command with its pipe operators, and the answer. Ze writes under $HOME/.local/share while XDG_DATA_HOME is unset, and it reports a directory it cannot create on stderr. Daemon settings The container holds the path of the PID file and the user Ze changes to. Ze reads both leaves at startup, in that order, and neither one changes a running daemon. PID file path Ze writes its own process ID to this path at startup and removes the file at a clean shutdown. The create refuses an existing file, so a second daemon that names the same path stops at startup with an error. When the user leaf is also set, Ze gives the file to that user, because the shutdown path runs after the change of user. Ze writes no PID file while the leaf is absent. System user for privilege drop Ze starts as root to bind port 179, then changes to this user before it starts a plugin or accepts a connection. A user name and a numeric UID are both accepted, and the user's primary group is used. Ze keeps root while the leaf is absent. ExaBGP compatibility settings for the migration bridge The bridge runs an unchanged ExaBGP API program against Ze, and the container holds the settings of the channel to that program. ExaBGP bridge API settings The con

title: exabgp
text: exabgp bridge add-path enumeration family address-family process <name> encoder enumeration feed <peer> event string respawn boolean run string route-refresh boolean Top-level container for ExaBGP-compatibility configuration. The bridge itself lives in the bridge container under this root, which keeps the root free for other ExaBGP compatibility settings. The plugin is registered as exabgp-bridge, so plugin { internal exabgp-bridge } starts it. The bridge refuses to start until bridge run names a script. In-process ExaBGP bridge settings. Present this container to configure the internal exabgp-bridge plugin. ADD-PATH mode for the families the bridge negotiates. RFC 7911 defines ADD-PATH. none disables it. receive accepts more than one path from the peer. send advertises more than one path to the peer. both does each of the two. Address families the bridge negotiates for the script. One example is ipv4/unicast. If this leaf-list is empty, the bridge negotiates ipv4/unicast. One ExaBGP-format script the bridge runs as a subprocess. One block per script. An ExaBGP configuration declares the same set as 'process <name> { run ... }', and the migration writes one block here for each of them. Ze starts every block, sends every event to every script, and reads commands from every script. The bridge does nothing until one block names a run command. Format the script's events are written in. json writes one JSON object per event. text writes ExaBGP's one-event-per-line format, such as 'neighbor 127.0.0.1 receive update announced 10.0.0.0/24 next-hop 10.0.0.1 origin igp'. ExaBGP spells this leaf the same way and declares it per process, so one bridge can feed a text script and a JSON script at once. The default is json because the envelope Ze declares is 6.0.0, and ExaBGP 6 answers every process in JSON. One peer that feeds this script, and the events it feeds. An ExaBGP neighbor names the processes it feeds in 'api { processes [ ... ] }' and the message kinds it feeds them in the same block, so the relation is per peer AND per script. The migration writes one block here for each neighbor that named this script. Ze also sends a command that names no neighbor to these peers alone. A process with NO feed block is fed by every peer with every event, which is what one script and one neighbor means. Events this peer feeds this script. ExaBGP's own event names: 'receive-update', 'send-update', 'receive-open', 'send-keepalive', 'receive-notification', 'send-refresh', 'receive-operational' and their siblings, plus 'neighbor-changes', 'negotiated', 'fsm' and 'signal'. An EMPTY list feeds no event from this peer, which is what an ExaBGP api block that names a process and no message kind does. Start the script again when it exits. true starts the script again the moment it exits. false leaves it stopped, which is what a script that does its work once and exits needs. A script that exits more than five times in 64 seconds stays stopped whatever this leaf holds, and Ze logs that it did. ExaBGP spells this leaf the same way and applies the same limit. Command line of the script. Two examples are './plugin.py' and 'python3 /opt/plugin.py'. Ze splits the line on whitespace. The first token is the executable, and the rest are its arguments. A block with no run command is refused. Advertise the BGP route-refresh capability. RFC 2918 defines the route-refresh capability. When this leaf is true, Ze advertises the capability on every session the bridge feeds.

title: fib
text: fib kernel flush-on-stop boolean sweep-delay uint16 p4 device-id uint64 flush-on-stop boolean target string vpp batch-interval-ms uint16 batch-size uint16 enabled boolean table-id uint32 Forwarding Information Base configuration. The FIB is where Ze writes the best routes the system RIB chose. Each container under it is one backend: kernel programs the OS with netlink, and vpp programs VPP with the GoVPP binary API. A backend runs only while its plugin is loaded. Admin distance is not here, because it belongs to the rib container. OS kernel route programming via netlink (Linux). Ze writes each best route from the system RIB into the OS with netlink, and it stamps rtm_protocol 250 on every route it writes. That number separates a ze route from a route another daemon owns, so `ip route show proto 250` lists them. The plugin also watches the kernel, and it writes its route again where something else overwrote one of them. Remove every ze-installed route when the plugin stops. When true, the plugin removes every route it installed as it stops. The default false keeps those routes in the kernel after shutdown, which supports graceful restart. Time to wait after startup before Ze sweeps stale routes. The delay lets BGP reconverge and refresh the matching routes before Ze removes the stale ones. The default is 30 seconds. P4 switch route programming via gRPC/P4Runtime. fib-p4 subscribes to the best-change event of the system RIB and holds every route it would program into a P4 switch with P4Runtime. The gRPC client is not written yet. The plugin writes a log line for each route it adds, replaces and deletes, and it programs no switch. The command `show fib p4` prints the prefix and the next hop of each entry the plugin holds. No leaf in this container reaches a switch today. P4Runtime device ID. P4Runtime addresses one forwarding pipeline on a target by its device id, and the switch assigns that number. The default 1 matches a target that carries one pipeline. The type is a 64-bit unsigned number. The plugin opens no P4Runtime session yet, so the value reaches no switch. Remove all forwarding entries when the plugin stops. When true, the plugin deletes every forwarding entry it installed as it stops. The default false leaves those entries in the switch after shutdown, which supports graceful restart. The plugin does not read this leaf yet: the stop path keeps the entries whatever you write, and the backend programs no switch. The kernel backend carries the same leaf at fib/kernel/flush-on-stop. P4Runtime gRPC target address (host:port). Example: 127.0.0.1:9559 The value names the P4Runtime gRPC server on the switch as host:port, and 9559 is the port P4Runtime listens on by convention. There is no default, so the leaf stays unset until you write it. The plugin opens no connection to this address yet, because the gRPC client is not written. VPP FIB programming via GoVPP binary API. Ze writes each best route from the system RIB into the VPP FIB with the GoVPP call IPRouteAddDel. The plugin needs a live VPP connector. With none it falls back to a backend that programs nothing and writes a warning. Ze asks the system RIB to replay the whole table each time VPP connects, so a VPP restart reprograms every route. Maximum time in milliseconds before dispatching a partial batch. The leaf declares how long a partial batch would wait before dispatch, in milliseconds, and the plugin implements no batching. A config that writes this leaf fails to parse, with an error naming batch-interval-ms as not yet implemented, so the default 10 never applies. The leaf batch-size is deferred for the same reason. Maximum number of routes per batch dispatch. The leaf declares how many routes one batch dispatch would carry, and the plugin implements no batching. A config that writes this leaf fails to parse, with an error naming batch-size as not yet implemented, so the default 256 never applies. The system RIB already delivers one batch per address family, and the VPP call IPRouteAddDel programs one route per call. The plugin programs each route as it arrives. Enable VPP FIB programming. Routes from system RIB are programmed directly into VPP's FIB. The plugin programs the VPP FIB for as long as it runs, and it does not read this leaf. The config parser accepts the name and stores no value. Programming starts when the plugin loads and stops when it unloads, so the default false disables nothing. Unload the fib-vpp plugin to stop programming the VPP FIB. VRF table ID for route programming. 0 is the default VRF. The value names the VPP VRF that Ze programs, and the default 0 is the default VRF. Ze gives it to the IP backend and to the MPLS and SRv6 backends at the moment it builds them. A new value reaches VPP when the plugin builds a backend again, which happens when VPP connects.

title: firewall
text: firewall backend string domain-group <name> domain-names string ttl-floor uint32 flush-on-shutdown boolean global-options all-ping enumeration broadcast-ping enumeration ipv6-receive-redirects enumeration ipv6-src-route enumeration log-martians enumeration receive-redirects enumeration send-redirects enumeration source-validation enumeration syn-cookies enumeration irr interface <name> source-as-set string peeringdb-url string refresh-interval uint32 server string table <name> chain <name> hook chain-hook policy chain-policy priority int32 term <name> from connection-mark mark-value connection-state connection-state destination-address ip-prefix destination-as-set string destination-asn asn destination-domain-group string destination-port port-spec dscp dscp-value icmp-type string icmpv6-type string input-interface string mark mark-value output-interface string protocol protocol-name source-address ip-prefix source-as-set string source-asn asn source-domain-group string source-port port-spec then accept connection-mark-set value mark-value counter name string dnat to nat-spec drop dscp-set dscp-value exclude flow-offload flowtable string goto string jump string limit-rate burst uint32 rate rate-spec log level uint32 prefix string mark-set value mark-value masquerade persistent empty port-range string random full empty notrack redirect to port reject code uint8 with reject-type return snat to nat-spec tcp-mss-set uint16 type chain-type family table-family flowtable <name> device string hook chain-hook priority int32 set <name> element <value> timeout uint32 flags-constant flags-dynamic flags-interval flags-timeout type set-type Ze-managed nftables firewall tables. Ze-managed nftables firewall tables. Table names are bare in config, and the component adds the ze_ prefix. Firewall backend implementation, nft by default. Firewall backend implementation. The default is nft, which is nftables through libnftnl. A future backend can declare itself through firewall.RegisterBackend. The ze:backend YANG extension on feature nodes declares per-feature backend support, so the commit-time gate rejects a config that uses an unsupported primitive. Address group whose members are what its DNS names resolve to. Ze resolves each name in the group and puts the addresses into an nftables set a rule can match with source-domain-group or destination-domain-group. Each name is resolved again when its own answer expires, and the set is reprogrammed only when the addresses changed. A commit naming a group Ze has never resolved is refused: run 'update firewall domain-group <name>' first. A permit rule keyed on a DNS name trusts whoever controls that name. DNS names whose addresses are the members of this group. Ze asks for the A and the AAAA record of each name and puts every address it gets into the group. Each name and each family keeps its own schedule, so a name with a short TTL does not pull the others with it. Ze accepts at most 64 addresses from one name and one family, and logs a warning when it drops the rest. Shortest interval Ze waits before it resolves a name again. A name answering with a very short TTL would otherwise drive a query and a set rewrite every few seconds. Ze waits this long at least, whatever the answer says. A TTL of 0 means 'do not cache' and Ze also waits the floor for it, rather than treating it as already expired. Remove ze-owned nftables tables when the ze process stops in an orderly way. Remove ze-owned nftables tables from the kernel when the ze process stops in an orderly way (SIGTERM). The default is true, so a stopped daemon leaves no rules behind. Set the leaf to false to use ze as a one-shot provisioner: program the rules, let the process exit, and leave them running in the kernel, like nft -f. The leaf keys off how the process exits, and it is unrelated to BGP graceful restart. A crash never runs the shutdown path, so tables always persist across a crash whatever this leaf holds. The leaf governs every ze table producer (firewall, control-plane-protection, policy-routes, ddos-local), which share one backend. Network security defaults mapped to kernel sysctls. Network security defaults mapped to kernel sysctls. The container provides VyOS-compatible keyword toggles for common settings. At apply time each keyword translates to a sysctl key and value pair emitted to the sysctl plugin. An explicit sysctl setting always overrides these. Control ICMP echo (ping) responses. The keyword writes net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_all. The sysctl is inverted, so enable writes 0 and disable writes 1. A router set to disable answers no ICMP echo request. A monitoring system that pings it sees no reply. Control broadcast ICMP echo responses. Control broadcast ICMP echo responses. The sysctl is inverted, so enable sets icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 0. Control acceptance of IPv6 ICMP redirect messages. The keyword writes net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. The leaf governs IPv6 alone. The IPv4 sysctl stays under receive-redirects. Control acceptance of IPv6 packets with source routing headers. The keyword writes net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A source-routed packet carries a routing header that names hops it MUST pass. An accepted one lets the sender pick the path through this router. Log packets with impossible source addresses. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A martian packet carries a source address that no route can reach. The kernel writes one line for each such packet, and a flood of them fills the log. Control acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirect messages. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. An accepted ICMP redirect installs a host route in the kernel. A neighbor on the same segment can then change where this router sends the traffic. Control sending of IPv4 ICMP redirect messages. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A router sends an ICMP redirect when it forwards a packet back out the interface the packet arrived on. Reverse path filtering mode for source address validation. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter. The value disable writes 0, strict writes 1, and loose writes 2. Strict drops a packet when the best route back to its source does not use the interface it arrived on. Loose drops it only when no route back to the source exists. TCP SYN cookie protection against SYN flood attacks. The keyword writes net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A kernel with cookies on answers a SYN that overflows the accept queue. It keeps no state for that half-open connection until the third packet returns the cookie. IRR policy settings for firewall prefix-list resolution. The settings under it reach every IRR reference of the firewall, in a term and on an interface alike. Ze keeps the resolved prefixes in a zefs prefix store that the BGP IRR filter shares, so one query serves both. A commit that names a reference with no cached prefixes is refused. Per-interface AS-SET binding for ingress source validation. Ze drops a packet that arrives on this interface when its source address is not in the IRR-resolved prefixes of the AS-SET. AS-SET whose IRR-resolved prefixes are the allowed source addresses. The prefixes the IRR resolves for this AS-SET form the allowed source-address set of the interface. The match needs cached prefix data. A config commit is refused when no cached data exists. Base URL for PeeringDB API queries. Override for testing with a mock server. The default is https://www.peeringdb.com. Ze adds /api/net?asn=<N> to this value for each query, and holds each answer for one hour. Ze skips TLS verification for the host 127.0.0.1 alone, which is what makes a local test server work. Seconds between automatic IRR re-queries. The default 0 disables the automatic refresh, and the operator then runs 'update firewall irr' by hand. A value in 60..86400 starts the periodic refresh. That refresh fails closed: a failed query keeps the last-good cache. IRR whois server hostname or host:port. The default is whois.radb.net. Ze adds port 43 when the value names no port, so a host:port value reaches the port you name. One query waits 10 seconds at most, and Ze holds each answer for one hour. Named firewall table The kernel table is ze_<name>. Ze changes and deletes only a table that carries the ze_ prefix, so a table another tool wrote stays untouched. The chains, the named sets and the flowtables of one table reference each other by name, and no reference crosses a table. Named chain within table A chain that carries a type or a hook is a base chain, and the kernel attaches it to that hook. A chain with neither is a regular chain, and only a jump or a goto from another chain of the same table reaches it. Netfilter hook point (base chains only) A base chain MUST carry a hook, and verify refuses one that does not. The hook decides where in the kernel path the chain sees the packet. The values input, output, forward, prerouting and postrouting serve every family. The value ingress serves a netdev or inet table, and egress serves a netdev table. Default policy (base chains only) The policy decides a packet that reaches the end of the chain with no verdict from a term. A base chain MUST carry accept or drop, and verify refuses a base chain that carries neither. A regular chain takes no policy, and the packet returns to the chain that jumped to it. Chain priority (base chains only) The chain with the lower number runs first at the same hook. Verify accepts -400 to 400 and refuses a number outside that range, which catches a typo such as 500 for 50. The well-known nftables values all fit: raw -300, mangle -150, filter 0, security 50, nat prerouting -100 and nat postrouting 100. An absent leaf means 0. Named rule (from/then structure) The list is ordered-by user, and the backend writes one kernel rule for each term in that order. A term MUST carry at least one action, and verify refuses one that carries none. Match criteria Every match in this container MUST hold at the same time for the term to act, because they lower into one kernel rule. A from block that declares no match matches every packet the chain sees. Connection mark value with an optional mask. The mark lives on the conntrack entry, so every packet of one flow reads the same value in both directions. The mark leaf beside it reads the per-packet mark instead, which starts at 0 for each packet. The match is conntrack-driven, and it needs a backend that integrates with the kernel nf_conntrack module. Connection tracking state(s) the rule matches. Connection tracking state(s). The match is conntrack-driven, and it requires a backend that integrates with the kernel nf_conntrack module. Destination IP prefix or @set-name The value takes the same two forms the source-address leaf takes. Ze reads the IPv4 destination at network-header offset 16 and the IPv6 destination at offset 24. An inet table therefore carries an nfproto guard in front of the match, so an IPv4 rule never reads IPv6 bytes. Match the destination address against the IRR-resolved prefixes of this AS-SET. The cache rule is the one source-as-set states. The match needs cached prefix data, so run 'update firewall irr as-set <name>' first. A config commit is refused when no cached data exists. Match the destination address against the IRR-resolved prefixes of this ASN. The cache rule is the one source-asn states. The match needs cached prefix data, so run 'update firewall irr asn <N>' first. A config commit is refused when no cached data exists. Match the destination address against the addresses of this domain group. The cache rule is the one source-domain-group states. The match needs the group's names to have resolved at least once,

title: flow-export
text: flow-export collector <name> address ip-address agent-address ip-address max-datagram-size uint16 observation-domain uint32 polling-interval uint16 port uint16 protocol enumeration source-address ip-address sub-agent-id uint32 template-refresh uint32 conntrack active-timeout uint16 enabled boolean recent-flow-ring uint32 enrichment bgp boolean sampling interface <name> group uint32 rate uint32 trunc-size uint16 Flow export (sFlow, NetFlow v9, IPFIX) configuration Flow export configuration. Ze exports interface counters to every collector. It exports per-flow records as well when the conntrack container or the sampling container is enabled. Each collector names its own protocol, so one device can feed an sFlow collector and an IPFIX collector at the same time. A flow export collector endpoint A flow export collector endpoint. Ze opens one UDP sender for each entry and encodes for the protocol that entry names. address and protocol are both mandatory, so a commit that leaves either one out is rejected. max-datagram-size bounds each UDP payload, including padding. Collector IP address Collector IP address, and the leaf is mandatory. The address and port together are where Ze sends every datagram of this collector. A commit that gives a value Ze cannot parse as an address is rejected. sFlow agent address (device's own stable IP, e.g. loopback) sFlow agent address, which is the device's own stable IP address. Ze writes it into the sFlow v5 datagram header, so a collector identifies the exporter by one address whichever interface the datagram left. It is mandatory on an sflow collector, 0.0.0.0 and :: are refused, and all sflow collectors must name the same address, because Ze is one sFlow agent. Two spellings of one address, such as 2001:db8::1 and 2001:DB8:0::1, are the same address. A netflow9 or ipfix collector does not read the leaf. Largest UDP payload sent to this collector, in octets Largest UDP payload Ze sends to this collector, in octets. Encoders include padding within this bound. RFC 7011 Section 10.3.3 recommends packets of at most 512 octets when the path MTU is unknown. The default 464 reserves 48 octets for IPv6 and UDP headers. Set a larger value only for a known path MTU, after subtracting all IP, UDP and tunnel headers. The ceiling 1400 is the encoding buffer size. IPFIX/NetFlow v9 observation domain ID IPFIX and NetFlow v9 observation domain ID, default 0. Ze writes it into the message header of every counter message and every flow message of those two protocols. A collector uses it to keep the record streams of one exporter apart. An sflow collector does not read the leaf. Counter polling interval in seconds Counter polling interval in seconds, 1 to 3600, default 20. The interval is a maximum: Ze sends the interface counters to this collector at least once in each interval. Counter snapshots arrive once a second, so Ze polls from one second before the interval ends. The counter snapshot is shared between collectors, so a short interval on one collector does not make another one faster. Collector UDP port Collector UDP port. The default 6343 is the port sFlow collectors listen on, so a NetFlow v9 or an IPFIX collector usually needs its own port written here. The port is per collector, so two entries can send to one address on two ports. Export protocol Export protocol, and the leaf is mandatory. The value selects the encoder Ze builds for this collector. It also decides which of the other leaves are read. sub-agent-id and agent-address are read by sflow alone, and observation-domain by netflow9 and ipfix alone. Source IP address for outbound flow export datagrams Source IP address for outbound flow export datagrams. Ze binds the UDP socket of this collector to the address. Left out, the kernel selects a source from its route to the collector. The value does not reach the sFlow datagram header, which carries agent-address instead. sFlow sub-agent identifier sFlow sub-agent identifier, default 0. Ze writes it into the sFlow v5 datagram header. It separates several sFlow agents that share one agent-address, so a collector can keep their sequence numbers apart. Every sflow collector exports every interface, and sFlow v5 binds each data source to one sub-agent, so all sflow collectors must name the same value: the config is refused otherwise. A netflow9 or ipfix collector does not read the leaf. Template refresh interval in seconds (NetFlow v9, IPFIX) Template refresh interval in seconds, 1 to 86400, default 600. NetFlow v9 and IPFIX resend the record template on this interval, so a collector that restarts can decode the records again. The counter template and the flow template each keep their own timer. The sFlow encoder has no template and does nothing with the value. Per-flow record export from conntrack (NetFlow v9, IPFIX) Per-flow record export from conntrack. Ze dumps the kernel conntrack table on a timer and turns each live entry into a flow record for the NetFlow v9 and IPFIX collectors. The same records fill the recent-flow ring that 'show flow recent' and the DDoS characterization read. Seconds between conntrack table dumps Seconds between conntrack table dumps, 1 to 3600, default 60. Each dump turns the live conntrack entries into flow records. Ze also drops its own tracking state for a flow it has not seen for twice this time. A short timeout therefore shortens that memory too. Export per-flow records from the conntrack table Export per-flow records from the conntrack table. Left false, Ze starts no conntrack worker and allocates no recent-flow ring. 'show flow recent' then has nothing to read, and the DDoS characterization loses its flow input and falls back to its coarse target. Capacity of the recent-flow ring, in flow records. `show flow recent` reads the ring, and the ring feeds the on-box DDoS characterization. A larger value keeps more history and uses more memory. Ze allocates the ring only when conntrack export is enabled. Flow record enrichment from the BGP RIB Flow record enrichment from the BGP RIB. Ze keeps a prefix-to-AS radix tree that BGP best-path changes feed. A flow record reads its next hop and its AS numbers from that tree. The tree is swapped whole, so a record never reads a half-built tree. Enrich flow records with BGP next-hop (and AS where available) Enrich flow records with the BGP next hop, and with the AS numbers where the RIB carries them. Ze subscribes to the RIB best-path changes and rebuilds the lookup tree at most once per rebuild interval. A full-table replay event carries no AS_PATH, so those entries hold no AS until the next incremental change corrects them. Packet sampling (tc sample + psample) exported as sFlow flow samples Packet sampling exported as sFlow flow samples. Ze installs a tc sample action on each listed interface and reads the sampled headers from the kernel psample netlink family. The path is Linux only. A setup failure is logged and leaves that interface unsampled, and the rest of the exporter keeps running. Per-interface packet sampling configuration Per-interface packet sampling configuration. Ze installs the tc action for each entry on its own, so a failure on one entry does not stop another. Ze maps each sample the kernel delivers back to its entry by kernel interface index. psample group ID psample group ID, default 1. Ze writes it into the tc sample action, which tags each sample the kernel emits. Ze does not read it back. The reader joins the psample packets multicast group and maps each sample to its interface by index. This value therefore does not select which samples Ze reads. Sampling rate (1-in-N packets) Sampling rate, as one packet in N. The leaf has no default, so an entry that leaves it out fails the commit with 'rate 0 out of range 1-1000000'. Ze passes the value to the tc sample action, and the kernel does the sampling. Bytes of each sampled packet header to capture Bytes of each sampled packet header to capture, 64 to 1500, default 128. The tc sample action truncates the frame to this length before the kernel passes it up. A larger value carries more of the packet into the sFlow flow sample, and it costs more bandwidth toward the collector.
