text: isis hostname string interfaces interface <name> address-family <af> circuit-type enumeration enabled boolean hello-interval uint16 hold-multiplier uint8 level enumeration level-1 auth-key-chain string hello-interval uint16 hold-multiplier uint8 metric uint32 priority uint8 level-2 auth-key-chain string hello-interval uint16 hold-multiplier uint8 metric uint32 priority uint8 metric uint32 passive boolean priority uint8 key-chains <name> key <key-id> accept-lifetime end string start string algorithm enumeration secret string send-lifetime end string start string level enumeration level-1 auth-key-chain string level-2 auth-key-chain string lsp-lifetime uint16 lsp-refresh-interval uint16 net string overload boolean system-id string IS-IS routing instance configuration. The presence of this container starts the IS-IS component. At least one `net` leaf MUST be set for the engine to run. A commit with no net is accepted, and the engine then stays idle, opens no circuit and originates no LSP. Dynamic hostname this IS-IS instance advertises (RFC 5301 section 3). Dynamic hostname to advertise (RFC 5301 section 3). Printable 7-bit ASCII only, from space (0x20) to tilde (0x7e). Each dot-separated label is 1 to 63 octets and the whole name is at most 255 octets, including the separators (RFC 2181 section 11). One trailing dot is permitted. A non-ASCII name is refused, not converted. IS-IS-enabled interfaces. Only an interface with an entry here runs IS-IS. Ze opens no circuit on an interface that this list omits, so no adjacency forms on it and its connected prefixes reach no LSP. Per-interface IS-IS configuration. Ze opens one circuit for each entry that is enabled and not passive. A link that comes up after start opens its circuit at that moment, and a link that goes down closes it. The connected prefixes of an enabled entry become TLV 135 and TLV 236 reachability in the node's own LSP. Enable address families on this interface. An ipv6-unicast entry enables the interface's IPv6 addresses and prefixes. On any enabled interface it also adds IPv6 to the node-wide Protocols Supported set in every Hello and LSP. IPv4 is always supported. Both families use one SPF tree. Circuit type. broadcast, the default, runs the DIS election and sources a pseudo-node LSP when this IS wins. It advertises the LAN as one TLV 22 entry that points at the pseudo-node. It also sources a periodic CSNP while this IS is DIS. point-to-point runs no election and no pseudo-node. It sends a point-to-point hello with TLV 240 and one initial CSNP when the adjacency reaches Up. IS-IS enabled on this interface. The default is true, so an entry runs IS-IS without this leaf. A false value keeps the entry in the configuration and opens no circuit. It also stops the connected prefixes of the interface from reaching the node's own LSP, which a passive interface still advertises. Hello interval. Ze sends an IIH on this circuit at this period. The IIH carries a holding time of this value multiplied by `hold-multiplier`, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. A neighbor drops the adjacency when no IIH arrives inside the holding time it was told. A shorter interval detects a dead neighbor faster and costs more packets on the link. `level-1/hello-interval` and `level-2/hello-interval` replace it at one level. Hold time = hello-interval * hold-multiplier. Ze advertises `hello-interval` multiplied by this value as the holding time in each IIH, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. The default of 3 lets two hellos be lost before a neighbor drops the adjacency. The clamp means that no configuration can advertise a holding time of 0, which would time the adjacency out at once. `level-1/hold-multiplier` and `level-2/hold-multiplier` replace it at one level. Per-interface level override. This narrows the instance `level` for one circuit. l1 forms only a Level-1 adjacency on the circuit, l2 only a Level-2 adjacency, and l1-l2 forms both. The circuit floods LSPs and advertises its reachability only at the levels it forms. A level the instance `level` does not hold stays off whatever this leaf says. Level-1 per-interface overrides. The leaves here replace the circuit-wide value for Level-1 only. One circuit can then carry a different cost, a different DIS preference, a different Hello period or a different holding time at each level. A leaf that is not set keeps the circuit-wide value. A circuit that does not form Level-1 ignores the whole container. L1 per-interface (IIH) key-chain reference. The value names a `key-chains` entry. Ze then signs and verifies the Level-1 IIH on this circuit with that chain. RFC 5304 section 2 states that 'IS-IS Hello PDUs SHALL use the Link Level Authentication String'. This leaf covers the hello only. The LSP, CSNP and PSNP take the chain that `isis/level-1/auth-key-chain` names. L1 hello-interval override. Ze sends the Level-1 IIH at this period, in place of the circuit-wide `hello-interval`. A broadcast circuit runs one Hello timer for each level it forms, because the Level-1 and the Level-2 LAN IIH are separate PDUs sent to separate multicast groups. A point-to-point circuit sends one IIH that serves both levels, so it runs one Hello timer, and that timer takes this pair whenever the circuit forms Level-1. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L1 hold-multiplier override. Ze multiplies the Level-1 hello interval by this value and advertises the product as the holding time in each Level-1 IIH, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. It replaces the circuit-wide `hold-multiplier` for Level-1. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L1 wide metric override. Ze advertises this cost for the circuit in the Level-1 LSP, in place of `metric`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide metric. The value also becomes the metric of the connected prefixes the circuit contributes at Level-1. L1 DIS priority override. Ze uses this priority in the Level-1 DIS election, in place of `priority`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide priority, and so does the value 0: Ze reads an override only when it is more than 0. To ask for the lowest preference, set the circuit-wide `priority` to 0. Level-2 per-interface overrides. The leaves here replace the circuit-wide value for Level-2 only. One circuit can then carry a different cost, a different DIS preference, a different Hello period or a different holding time at each level. A leaf that is not set keeps the circuit-wide value. A circuit that does not form Level-2 ignores the whole container. L2 per-interface (IIH) key-chain reference. The value names a `key-chains` entry. Ze then signs and verifies the Level-2 IIH on this circuit with that chain. RFC 5304 section 2 states that 'IS-IS Hello PDUs SHALL use the Link Level Authentication String'. This leaf covers the hello only. The LSP, CSNP and PSNP take the chain that `isis/level-2/auth-key-chain` names. L2 hello-interval override. Ze sends the Level-2 IIH at this period, in place of the circuit-wide `hello-interval`. A broadcast circuit runs one Hello timer for each level it forms, because the Level-1 and the Level-2 LAN IIH are separate PDUs sent to separate multicast groups. A point-to-point circuit sends one IIH that serves both levels, so it runs one Hello timer, and that timer takes this pair only on a circuit that forms Level-2 alone. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L2 hold-multiplier override. Ze multiplies the Level-2 hello interval by this value and advertises the product as the holding time in each Level-2 IIH, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. It replaces the circuit-wide `hold-multiplier` for Level-2. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L2 wide metric override. Ze advertises this cost for the circuit in the Level-2 LSP, in place of `metric`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide metric. The value also becomes the metric of the connected prefixes the circuit contributes at Level-2. L2 DIS priority override. Ze uses this priority in the Level-2 DIS election, in place of `priority`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide priority, and so does the value 0: Ze reads an override only when it is more than 0. To ask for the lowest preference, set the circuit-wide `priority` to 0. Wide metric (RFC 5305). The circuit advertises this cost in TLV 22, and its connected prefixes advertise it in TLV 135 and TLV 236. RFC 5305 section 3 states that 'The metric octets are encoded as a 24-bit unsigned integer', which is the 1 to 16777215 range here. SPF adds the value once for each hop, so a lower value makes the circuit preferred. `level-1/metric` and `level-2/metric` replace it at one level. Advertise the interface but form no adjacencies. Ze opens no circuit for a passive interface, so it sends no hello and forms no adjacency. The connected prefixes of the interface still become TLV 135 and TLV 236 entries in the node's own LSP, at the metric `metric` sets. Use it on a loopback and on a customer LAN, where the prefix MUST be reachable and no IS-IS neighbor exists. DIS election priority (broadcast circuits). The value rides in each LAN hello and decides the DIS election on a broadcast circuit. The highest priority wins, and the highest SNPA MAC address breaks a tie. A priority of 0 is valid and only lowers the preference, so it does not stop this IS from winning an election it is alone in. The leaf changes nothing on a point-to-point circuit. Named authentication key chains for hitless key rotation. A chain holds the keys that sign and verify IS-IS PDUs. Ze authenticates nothing until an `auth-key-chain` leaf names the chain. Ze refuses the configuration when an `auth-key-chain` leaf names no entry of this list, because a circuit whose chain does not resolve sends and accepts every PDU unsigned. A key whose algorithm token Ze does not know, or whose secret does not decode, is dropped from the chain and signs nothing. Keys in this chain. Ze reads the keys in configuration order, which is key-id order. The first key whose send lifetime holds the current time signs a PDU. Every key whose accept lifetime holds that time is accepted on receive, up to 16 keys, which is what makes a rotation lose no adjacency. When this key is accepted on receive (hitless rotation). Ze accepts a received PDU signed with any key whose accept window holds the current time, up to 16 keys in one chain. Open the accept window of the new key before its send window. Every neighbor then accepts the new key before any of them signs with it. RFC3339 end timestamp. The format is RFC 3339, for example 2026-06-01T00:00:00Z. An empty value leaves the end open. Keep the accept window of the old key open until every neighbor signs with the new key. RFC3339 start timestamp. The format is RFC 3339, for example 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z. An empty value leaves the start open, so the key is accepted from the moment it is committed. A value Ze cannot parse also leaves the start open. Authentication algorithm. cleartext sends the secret in the PDU as auth type 1, so it detects a misconfiguration and stops no attacker. hmac-md5, the default, is auth type 54 (RFC 5304). The five SHA choices are auth type 3 (RFC 5310) and range from HMAC-SHA-1 to HMAC-SHA-512. Ze drops a key whose token it does not know, so a typo here leaves that key out of the chain. Shared secret, masked and $9$-encoded at rest. The commit encodes the value with the reversible $9$ encoding, the same one PPPoE and WireGuard use, and the configuration output masks it. Ze decodes it in memory to derive the HMAC key. A value that does not decode drops the key from the chain. Both ends of an adjacency MUST hold the same plaintext secret under the same key-id. When this key may be used to sign (hitless rotation). Ze signs with the first key in the chain whose send window holds the current time. A key with no send-lifetime signs from the moment it is committed. When no key in the chain has an open send window, Ze sends the PDU unsigned, and a neighbor under authentication rejects it. RFC3339 end timestamp. The forma

title: kernel
text: kernel Kernel route redistribution. Presence enables the plugin. The container carries no leaf, so writing it is the whole configuration. The plugin watches the kernel routing table and emits each route on the redistribute event bus. A route whose netlink protocol is RTPROT_KERNEL or RTPROT_REDIRECT is dropped, so a connected subnet route and an ICMP redirect route never reach BGP. The plugin registers the kernel route source, and a redistribute statement names that source.

L2TPv2 tunnel subsystem settings (RFC 2661). Presence of this block with any content implies the subsystem is enabled. Use 'enabled false' to disable it explicitly, or 'enabled true' as a filler when no other settings are needed. Allow PPP LCP to finish with no Auth-Protocol, false by default. Allow PPP LCP authentication negotiation to proceed without an Auth-Protocol. The default is false, so a peer that rejects all configured authentication methods is disconnected, instead of being accepted as no-auth. PPP authentication for L2TP subscriber sessions. The container holds the backend that answers a credential. The l2tp-auth-local plugin fills the local container under it, and the l2tp-auth-radius plugin fills the radius container. The timing of the PPP authentication phase sits under l2tp authentication instead. Authenticate a subscriber against users declared in this config. Ze rejects every session while no user is declared here, and it logs that no user is configured. A session is matched against the list by its PPP username, and an unknown username is rejected. Local authentication answers PAP and CHAP-MD5, and it rejects MS-CHAPv2. One subscriber account, keyed by its PPP username. Ze looks the PPP username up in this list and rejects a username no entry carries. An empty list rejects every session. The match is exact, so user and user@example.net are two accounts. Shared secret for PAP cleartext and CHAP-MD5/MS-CHAPv2 challenge-response. PAP compares the SHA-256 of the received password with the SHA-256 of this value, in constant time. CHAP-MD5 computes MD5 over the identifier, this value and the challenge, which RFC 1994 Section 4.1 defines. CHAP needs the secret in clear, so this leaf holds no hash. Authenticate and account subscriber sessions against a RADIUS server. Authentication and accounting are separate exchanges to the same server. A session is authorized by an Access-Accept, and the Accounting-Request packets that follow report its traffic. Accounting interim-update interval in seconds. RFC 2869 Section 2.1 states that a locally configured value on the NAS MUST override the value found in an Access-Accept. A leaf that is set pins the cadence of every session, and the Acct-Interim-Interval attribute (type 85) of an Access-Accept then changes nothing. This leaf has no default. An unset leaf is the absent case, and it lets each Access-Accept set the cadence of that session. A session runs at 300 seconds when neither side states an interval. Which optional RADIUS attributes Ze puts in the packets it sends. Ze sends every attribute it can build, which is what a billing system usually wants, so this container is empty in most deployments. It names the attributes one deployment does not want on the wire. Nothing here reaches Acct-Status-Type, Acct-Session-Id or the NAS identity: RFC 2866 Section 5.13 counts the first two as 'Exactly one instance of this attribute MUST be present', and its Note 1 requires either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier, so an Accounting-Request without them is not a conformant record and Ze offers no way to write one. Attributes Ze does not send, each with the record types it is held back from. Name an attribute to hold it back from every record type that would carry it. Add packet-type under it to hold it back from some record types and keep it in the others. Each attribute accepts only the record types Ze can put it in, so a line naming a record type that never carries the attribute is refused when the configuration is committed rather than ignored at run time. Do not send Acct-Delay-Time (attribute 41). RFC 2866 Section 5.2 reports how many seconds the client has been trying to send this record, and Ze rewrites the value on each retransmission. A record that carries no Acct-Delay-Time is replayed byte for byte instead, under the same Identifier, which is what an Access-Request does. accel-ppp ships this attribute off by default. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Acct-Delay-Time in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send Acct-Terminate-Cause (attribute 49). RFC 2866 Section 5.10 states that the attribute 'can only be present in Accounting-Request records where the Acct-Status-Type is set to Stop', so the Stop record is the only one this reaches. A pipeline that keys on its own teardown signal does not need it. FreeRADIUS defaults it to NAS-Reboot in its accounting queries. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. RFC 2866 Section 5.10 admits Acct-Terminate-Cause in a Stop record alone, so accounting-stop is the one value this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from the Stop record, which is the same thing said with fewer words. Do not send Calling-Station-Id (attribute 31). RFC 2865 Section 5.31 carries the number the call came from, which is the L2TP Calling Number of the session, or the subscriber MAC address on the PPPoE relay path. Some operators do not store it. Check the server first: FreeRADIUS matches its IP pool queries on this attribute with no fallback value, so a pool it serves keeps leases that never expire once the attribute stops arriving. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Calling-Station-Id in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send Event-Timestamp (attribute 55). RFC 2869 Section 5.3 records the second at which the event happened on the NAS. A server that stamps its own receive time does not need it. FreeRADIUS falls back to the server clock in its default accounting queries, so a record without the attribute is still stored with a time. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Event-Timestamp in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send Framed-IP-Address (attribute 8). RFC 2865 Section 5.8 reports the IPv4 address the session negotiated, and RFC 2866 Section 4.1 requires that a record which carries the attribute carries the real address. An operator whose addressing is reported by another system can hold it back. A session with no IPv4 address sends no attribute either way, which is a different case and is not configurable. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Framed-IP-Address in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send NAS-Port-Id (attribute 87). RFC 2869 Section 5.17 names the access port in text, and the nas-port-id-format leaf is the template Ze resolves for it. Clearing that leaf also sends no attribute, on every packet at once. This container is the finer instrument: it holds the attribute back from the record types you name while the template stays configured for the rest. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts NAS-Port-Id in the Access-Request and in the three accounting records, so all four are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all four. UDP port of the RADIUS CoA and Disconnect listener, usually 3799. The listener implements RFC 5176. This leaf has no default on purpose. An unset leaf keeps the listener off, so an existing deployment does not start to accept CoA on upgrade. Ze accepts a request only from a configured RADIUS server address. NAS-Identifier sent in RADIUS requests. Ze sends this text as the NAS-Identifier attribute in each Access-Request and each Accounting-Request. RFC 2865 Section 4.1 requires either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier in an Access-Request. With this leaf empty and source-address empty, Ze sends the hostname, and the plugin name where the host carries none. Template for the NAS-Port-Id attribute sent in RADIUS requests. Ze sends the NAS-Port-Id attribute (RFC 2869 Section 5.17) in an Access-Request packet and in an Accounting-Request packet. The placeholders are {nas-id}, {tunnel-id} and {session-id}. Ze copies every other character. All three values are known before the session has an interface. One session therefore sends one text in its Access-Request and in all its accounting records. A billing system can join them on it. The 253-octet limit is the largest value a RADIUS attribute can carry (RFC 2865 Section 5). The commit refuses an unknown placeholder, it refuses a {nas-id} when nas-identifier is unset, and it refuses a template whose widest resolution passes 253 octets because the nas-identifier it expands is long. An unset leaf sends no attribute. Discard a CoA-Request or a Disconnect-Request that carries no Message-Authenticator. RFC 5176 Section 3.4 makes the Message-Authenticator attribute optional, so the default is false. Ze then processes a request without the attribute once its Request Authenticator verifies against the shared secret. Set this leaf to true when every Dynamic Authorization Client sends the attribute. The attribute is an HMAC-MD5 keyed with the shared secret, and it is the mitigation for the Blast-RADIUS class of attack (CVE-2024-3596), which forges a RADIUS UDP packet with a chosen-prefix MD5 collision against the authenticator. A client that sends no attribute gets no answer while this leaf is true. Number of retransmit attempts per server. The default is 3 and the range is 1 to 10. Ze sends the request that many times to one server, then moves to the next entry of the list. An Access-Request is replayed byte for byte. An Accounting-Request gets a new identifier and a new Acct-Delay-Time on each attempt, which RFC 2866 Section 4.1 requires. One RADIUS server Ze sends requests to, tried in the order written. The operator orders the list. Ze tries the first entry, and moves to the next one when that server does not answer. Write the closest server first. RADIUS server IP address or hostname. The leaf is mandatory, and Ze refuses a server entry without it. Ze joins the value to port to reach the server. The first entry of the list is the one Ze tries first, so write the closest server first. RADIUS server UDP port. The default is 1812 and the range is 1 to 65535. Ze sends the Acces

title: ldp
text: ldp hello-hold-time uint16 hello-interval uint16 hop-count-max uint8 interfaces string keepalive-time uint16 lsr-id string transport-address string Label Distribution Protocol configuration The engine stays idle until lsr-id carries an address, and it says so in the log. Ze then sends Hello messages to 224.0.0.2 port 646 and opens a TCP session on port 646 to each neighbor it discovers. Hello adjacency hold time The default is 15 seconds, which is 3 hello intervals. Ze advertises this value in each Hello, and a neighbor drops the adjacency when no Hello arrives inside it. Keep it more than hello-interval, because a hold time under one interval drops the adjacency between two Hellos. Hello message interval The default is 5 seconds and the range is 1 to 65535. Ze sends one Hello for each interface at this period. A shorter interval finds a neighbor faster and puts more packets on the link. Maximum hop count a Label Mapping can carry. The default is 254 and the range is 1 to 255. RFC 5036 section 3.4.4.1 makes an LSR check the Hop Count TLV of a received message against 'its configured maximum allowable value'. A Label Mapping whose hop count exceeds this value is answered with a Loop Detected Notification and its label is not used. A change here applies to the sessions that open after it. Interfaces on which LDP discovery is enabled Ze runs one discovery listener for each interface of this list. An empty list runs one listener that the system assigns to an interface itself. A reload starts discovery on an interface added to the list and stops it on one removed, and it leaves the other interfaces alone. The connected prefixes of these interfaces are the FECs this LSR is egress for. Session keepalive interval. The default is 60 seconds and the range is 1 to 65535. RFC 5036 section 3.5.3 carries the KeepAlive Time in the Common Session Parameters of the Initialization message. The receiving LSR MUST calculate the KeepAlive Timer from 'the smaller of its proposed KeepAlive Time and the KeepAlive Time received in the PDU'. The lower of the two proposals wins. Ze proposes this value to each neighbor it opens a session to. Ze sends a KeepAlive every third of the negotiated value and closes the session when no PDU arrives inside three times it. The exchange happens one time, at the start of the session, so a session that is up keeps the value it negotiated. A change here applies to the sessions that open after it. LSR identifier (IPv4 address format) Ze refuses a value that is not an IP address, and stays idle while the leaf is empty. The first 4 bytes of every LDP PDU header carry this identifier. Ze also originates a label binding for the address itself, so a neighbor can reach this LSR by its identifier. Transport address for TCP sessions Ze advertises this address in the transport address TLV of each Hello, which is the address a neighbor connects to. Ze also binds it as the source address of the TCP connection it opens. With the leaf empty, the Hello carries no transport address TLV and the kernel picks the source address.

title: mrt
text: mrt add-path boolean all file string interval uint32 direction enumeration extended-timestamp boolean peer-filter string routes file string interval uint32 updates file string interval uint32 MRT dump configuration. The container holds the extended-timestamp switch, the add-path switch, the peer filter, the direction, and the three dump streams. Use ADD-PATH subtypes for RIB snapshots. The default is false. When true, TABLE_DUMP_V2 snapshots use the ADD-PATH RIB subtypes of RFC 8050. BGP4MP and BGP4MP_ET message subtypes always follow the direction-specific negotiated ADD-PATH state of the UPDATE family, independently of this leaf. All BGP messages and state changes, written as BGP4MP records. The stream carries every BGP message: OPEN, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION, KEEPALIVE and ROUTE_REFRESH. It carries the FSM state transitions too. Ze writes them as BGP4MP records. Output file path, with strftime patterns for rotation. The strftime codes in the path decide when Ze opens a new file. The supported codes are %Y (year), %m (month), %d (day), %H (hour), %M (minute), %S (second), %s (unix timestamp) and %N (table name). File rotation interval in seconds. Zero disables rotation. The value 0 keeps one file open until the daemon stops. A value of more than 0 makes Ze close the file once it has been open that many seconds. Ze then opens the next one, and the strftime codes in file give the new name. A file of - writes to standard output, which never rotates. Which direction of BGP messages to record. The default is both, and both records each direction. received keeps the messages the peer sent to Ze, and sent keeps the messages Ze sent to the peer. The filter reaches the BGP messages alone, so a state change record is written whatever the value. Use BGP4MP_ET (type 17) with microsecond resolution instead of BGP4MP (type 16). The default is false, so each record header carries type 16, BGP4MP. RFC 6396 Section 5.3 names type 17 as BGP4MP_ET, and that header carries 4 more bytes for the microsecond field. The switch reaches all three streams at once. If set, only record messages from/to these peer addresses. Empty list means record all peers. Ze compares each entry with the peer address of the message, so a message of another peer reaches no file. The filter reaches the BGP messages alone: Ze writes a state change record for every peer, whatever this list holds. Periodic RIB snapshots, written as TABLE_DUMP_V2 records. Each dump writes one PEER_INDEX_TABLE record, and then the RIB entries for every address family. Ze writes them as TABLE_DUMP_V2 records. Output file path with strftime patterns. The strftime codes in the path name the file Ze opens, exactly as they do in a dump stream. Ze writes this stream only when the path is set and interval is more than 0. A path of - writes to standard output. RIB dump interval in seconds. Minimum 60. The default is 3600 seconds and the range is 60 to 86400. Each dump writes one PEER_INDEX_TABLE record and then the RIB entries of every address family, which RFC 6396 Section 4.3.1 requires in that order. BGP UPDATE message stream (BGP4MP records). The stream carries the UPDATE messages alone. The all stream beside it carries every message type. Output file path, with strftime patterns for rotation. The strftime codes in the path decide when Ze opens a new file. The supported codes are %Y (year), %m (month), %d (day), %H (hour), %M (minute), %S (second), %s (unix timestamp) and %N (table name). File rotation interval in seconds. Zero disables rotation. The value 0 keeps one file open until the daemon stops. A value of more than 0 makes Ze close the file once it has been open that many seconds. Ze then opens the next one, and the strftime codes in file give the new name. A file of - writes to standard output, which never rotates.
