boolean interval uint32 maintenance-window end string start string restart immediate empty time string spread uint32 url string System-level settings The container holds the system-wide settings. This module attaches the local user accounts under authentication, and the command authorization profiles under authorization. Named config archive destinations. Each entry names one destination, and Ze writes a copy of the config to every entry its trigger fires for. Filename format with token substitution. The tokens are {name} for the config basename, {host}, {domain}, {date} as YYYYMMDD, {time} as HHMMSS, and {archive} for the block name. Ze appends .conf. Archive destination URL (file://, http://, https://). A file:// URL writes to the local filesystem. An http:// or https:// URL uploads the config with an HTTP request. Time-based only: skip if config unchanged since last archive. With true, Ze skips a daily or hourly archive when the config did not change since the last one. The leaf changes nothing for the commit trigger and the manual trigger. HTTP upload timeout, in Go duration format, for example 30s. Ze gives up on an upload that passes this timeout. The format is the Go duration format, such as 30s or 2m. When to archive. The triggers are commit, manual, daily and hourly. System authentication settings System authentication settings. The user list under it holds the local accounts, which the local AAA backend reads. That backend runs after TACACS+ in the chain, so it answers when the remote server is unreachable. A configuration with no user rejects every local login. RADIUS servers for operator login over SSH, web and MCP (RFC 2865). This block is separate from the L2TP subscriber RADIUS path, which lives under the l2tp root. Credential the Access-Request carries for an operator login. RFC 2865 Section 4.1 and RFC 3579 Section 3.3 Note 1 permit one credential and never two, so ze sends exactly one. Select chap only when the RADIUS server holds the operator password in cleartext. RFC 2865 Section 2.2 states that 'CHAP requires that the user's password be available in cleartext to the server so that it can encrypt the CHAP challenge and compare that to the CHAP response. If the password is not available in cleartext to the RADIUS server then the server MUST send an Access-Reject to the client.' A server that stores password hashes cannot verify CHAP and rejects every login. With pap the password is recoverable from a captured request by anyone who holds the shared secret, because Section 5.2 hides it with a reversible XOR. The two eap values run a full RADIUS/EAP conversation: ze answers EAP itself, as the peer, with the password the operator typed, and the server drives it through Access-Challenge packets. eap-md5 carries the same cleartext-password requirement as chap. eap-mschapv2 needs the server to hold the NT hash instead, which is what an Active Directory backed server holds. Ze authorization profiles used when the Access-Accept carries no profile-attribute. This leaf is optional. Leave it unset when the RADIUS server always names a profile through profile-attribute. When the server does not name one, and no default is set here, the login names no profile and is denied. Ze never authorizes a user it cannot attach a profile to. Access-Accept reply attribute that names the user's ze authorization profiles. Filter-Id is the only value. RFC 2865 Section 5.25 says of Class that 'the client MUST NOT interpret the attribute locally', so ze cannot read a profile name out of Class. Transmit attempts per server before failover The value counts the transmissions Ze sends to one server, and not the retransmissions after the first. With the default 3, Ze sends the Access-Request and retransmits it twice before it moves to the next server. The range is 0 to 10, and a configured 0 reaches the client as 3, because the client reads 0 as unset. The budget that bounds one login can then cancel the exchange partway through those transmissions. The login falls through to the local accounts, which is the answer a slow server gets too. Read timeout for the wait between the transmissions. RADIUS servers, tried in configured order Ze sends the Access-Request to the first server, and it moves to the next one when that server does not answer. The order is the config order, because the list is ordered-by user. Each server gets a new Identifier, a new Request Authenticator, and the User-Password hidden again under the key of that server. RFC 2865 Section 4.1 requires the new Request Authenticator: 'The Request Authenticator value MUST be changed each time a new Identifier is used.' Where every server fails, the AAA chain moves on to the local accounts, so an unreachable server never locks the operator out. A row that carries no key builds no RADIUS backend at all, rather than a shorter server list. RADIUS shared secret (RFC 2865). RFC 2865 Section 3 states that the secret MUST NOT be empty (length 0). An empty secret lets an attacker forge packets. UDP authentication port (default 1812) 1812 is the port officially assigned to RADIUS. RFC 2865 Section 3 states that 'Exactly one RADIUS packet is encapsulated in the UDP Data field, where the UDP Destination Port field indicates 1812 (decimal).' The range is 1 to 65535. Ze joins this port to the server address and resolves the pair as udp4. This block sends Access-Requests only, so it addresses the authentication port, and no accounting port is configured here. Source IP for outbound RADIUS requests Ze binds the outbound udp4 socket to this address, so every Access-Request leaves with it as the source. An IPv4 address here is also sent as NAS-IP-Address (RFC 2865 Section 4.1). Where the leaf is absent, the kernel picks the address of the outgoing interface and no NAS-IP-Address is sent. NAS-Identifier carries the hostname of this device either way, so the request meets Section 4.1 with the leaf unset. An address this host does not hold refuses the bind, and Ze logs the failure. The RADIUS backend then contributes nothing, and login falls through to the local accounts. Per-server request timeout in seconds The value bounds the wait for one answer from one server. Each wait after a miss doubles the one before it. The default 3 therefore waits 3 seconds, then 6, then 12, across the three transmissions the default retries allows. The range is 1 to 60 seconds. The time one login spends on RADIUS is capped at 2 minutes, whatever timeout and retries hold. The login then falls through to the local accounts. TACACS+ server configuration (RFC 8907) The TACACS+ backend joins the AAA chain at priority 100, in front of the local backend at priority 200. Ze builds the backend only where the server list holds one entry or more. Authorization or accounting selected without a server is a configuration error. Authentication runs as soon as one server exists. Authorization and accounting are selected independently. RFC 8907 Section 10.5 requires a network providing privacy, integrity and separation from other traffic. TACACS+ obfuscation and source-address selection do not provide those protections. Enable accounting for every entered command Set it true to account for every entered command, irrespective of its authorization method. A server is required. One worker sends START and STOP records from a bounded 64-record queue. A full queue delays command admission rather than losing a record; shutdown drains accepted records within the configured server timeout bounds. Transport failures are logged and do not deny command execution. Enable per-command TACACS+ authorization The default false authorizes each command from the local profiles alone and sends the server nothing. Set it true and Ze sends an AUTHOR REQUEST for each command, with service=shell, cmd=<verb> and one cmd-arg for each argument (RFC 8907 Section 6). PASS_ADD and PASS_REPL permit execution only when the effective arguments describe the original command and every mandatory policy can be enforced. FAIL refuses the command. Ze sends privilege level 1 on these requests. TACACS+ servers, tried in configured order Ze tries the servers in the order you write them and moves to the next one when a connection or an exchange fails. The order is the config order, because the list is ordered-by user. Where every server fails, the AAA chain moves on to the local backend, so the local accounts still answer. Shared secret this server obfuscates its packets with The key is the shared secret RFC 8907 Section 4.5 builds the MD5 pseudo-pad from, and both ends must hold the same value. A client with no secret has no conformant packet to send. Section 10.5.2 requires a shared secret and forbids a client to set TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG. Omitting the key refuses a commit, through the AAA rebuild rather than through the schema: a missing mandatory field is only a warning. At BOOT the same failure is logged and this backend is DROPPED from the chain. A user who exists locally still logs in, and the local profiles still govern the command. The leaf is sensitive, so display paths mask it. Keys of 32 characters or longer are supported. Use at least 16 characters; doctor warns about shorter keys. A $9$-encoded value is decoded on read; this is reversible obfuscation, not encryption. Protect configuration files, exports and backups as secrets. TCP port (default 49) Port 49 is the port IANA assigns to TACACS+, and RFC 8907 Section 3.4 names it. Ze opens one TCP connection to this port and reuses it where the server agrees to the single-connect flag. The type sets no lower bound, so a commit takes 0 and every connection to that server then fails. Source IP for outbound TACACS+ connections Ze binds the local end of the outbound TCP connection to this address. Use it where the TACACS+ server accepts one ad

title: telemetry
text: telemetry prometheus basic-auth enabled boolean password string plaintext-password string realm string username string collector <name> enabled boolean interval uint16 enabled boolean interval uint16 netdata collector <name> enabled boolean interval uint16 enabled boolean interval uint16 prefix string path string prefix string server <name> ip ip-address port listener-port Telemetry export configuration. The container holds the Prometheus export settings and the Netdata- compatible collector settings. Prometheus metrics HTTP export. The container holds the enable switch, the listen endpoints, the metrics path, the HTTP Basic Authentication settings and the collector settings. HTTP Basic Authentication for the Prometheus service. The container holds the enable switch, the realm, the username and the two password leaves. Require HTTP Basic Authentication on the metrics and health endpoints. Ze asks for no credentials while this leaf is false, and false is the default. Bcrypt-hashed HTTP Basic Authentication password. Write plaintext via plaintext-password. Ze compares the password of each request with this hash, and it compares the username in constant time. A value that is not a bcrypt hash stops the metrics server with an error, and the config check warns about it at commit. With basic-auth enabled, a username and this password are both required. Write-only password. On commit, the config system hashes this value into password and removes this leaf. The value is never written to the config file, and a display path renders the secret placeholder for it. HTTP Basic Authentication realm. A client shows the realm to the user when it asks for the credentials. The default is 'ze prometheus'. HTTP Basic Authentication username. The username pairs with the password leaf beside it. Deprecated: use netdata/collector. Per-Netdata-collector overrides (enable/disable, interval). Write netdata/collector instead. Ze reads this list only when the netdata container carries no collector list, and it then logs the deprecated path it read. A netdata collector list replaces this one whole, and the two are never merged. Enable or disable this collector. With false, Ze runs every other collector and stops this one. The default is true. Override sampling interval for this collector (seconds). Inherits global interval if not set. The range is 1 to 60 seconds. An absent leaf gives the collector the interval of the netdata container. The leaf lives under a deprecated list, so write netdata/collector/interval instead. Enable the Prometheus metrics endpoint. Ze serves no metrics endpoint while this leaf is false, and false is the default. Deprecated: use netdata/interval. Netdata-compatible OS collector sampling interval in seconds. Write netdata/interval instead. Ze reads this leaf only when the netdata container carries no interval leaf, and it then logs the deprecated path it read. The range is 1 to 60 seconds and the default is 1. Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics. These settings do not affect Ze-native metrics. The default of enabled is true, so an absent container still runs the collectors. The three settings under it replace the deprecated prefix, interval and collector leaves beside this container. Ze reads a deprecated leaf only when the matching leaf here is absent, and it logs the path it read. Per-Netdata-collector overrides of the enable state and the interval. Each entry names one collector, and it overrides the settings of that collector alone. Enable or disable this Netdata-compatible OS collector. With false, Ze runs every other collector and stops this one. The default is true. Override the sampling interval of this collector, in seconds. When this leaf is not set, the collector uses the global Netdata interval. Enable the Netdata-compatible OS collectors. With false, Ze exports the Ze-native metrics alone. The default is true. Netdata-compatible OS collector sampling interval in seconds. Each Netdata-compatible OS collector samples the operating system once in this interval. The range is 1 to 60 seconds, and the default is 1. Metric name prefix for Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics only. Ze puts the prefix in front of each Netdata-compatible OS collector metric name. It does not change a Ze-native metric name. The default is netdata. HTTP path of the metrics endpoint. A scraper reads the metrics at this path on each listen endpoint. The default path is /metrics. Deprecated: use netdata/prefix. The leaf sets the metric name prefix for Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics only. Prometheus listen endpoints. Each entry names one listen endpoint. The default endpoint is 127.0.0.1 on port 9273. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and an IPv4 address never overlaps an IPv6 address. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses.

title: traffic
text: traffic control backend string interface <name> qdisc class <name> ceil rate-bps match <type> value string priority uint8 rate rate-bps default-class string type qdisc-type usage enabled boolean interfaces interface <name> enabled boolean max-entries uint32 stale-timeout uint32 track-ip boolean interval uint32 max-entries uint32 stale-timeout uint32 track-ip boolean Traffic subsystem: QoS control and byte-usage accounting. Two subtrees sit under it, and they are independent. control programs the queueing disciplines of each interface, which decides which packet leaves first. usage counts bytes with an eBPF program, and it changes no packet. Each subtree comes from its own plugin, so removing one plugin removes that subtree alone. Traffic control configuration of each interface. One entry exists for each interface Ze programs. The backend leaf names the program that applies the entries. Traffic control backend that programs the queueing disciplines. The default backend is tc, the queueing disciplines of Linux iproute2. Another backend declares itself through traffic.RegisterBackend. The ze:backend YANG extension on a feature node declares which backend supports that feature. The commit-time gate reads that extension and rejects a config that names a qdisc or a filter type the backend does not support. Traffic control of one named interface. The list key is the interface name. The root queueing discipline of the interface. Ze attaches this qdisc at the root of the interface, and every class hangs beneath it. One traffic class of the queueing discipline. The list key is the class name. A class carries a rate, a ceil, a priority, and the filters that select its traffic. Largest rate this class can reach. An absent leaf takes the value of the rate leaf. A filter that classifies a packet into this class. The list key is the match type, so one class carries at most one match of each type. Value the filter matches. A mark filter takes a hex value. A dscp filter takes a DSCP name. A protocol filter takes a protocol name. Scheduling priority of this class. The value 0 is the highest priority. Rate this class is guaranteed. The value is a number and a unit, for example 10mbit or 100kbps. Name of the class that takes the unclassified traffic. The value is the name of a class in the class list of this qdisc. Type of the queueing discipline. The commit-time gate rejects a type the configured backend does not support. Per-interface eBPF TCX byte accounting (port/protocol always; per-IP via track-ip). Ze attaches two eBPF programs to each accounted interface with TCX, one on ingress and one on egress. They count bytes into per-interface LRU hash maps, keyed by L4 port and protocol. Where track-ip is true they also key by IPv4 address. One poll loop reads the maps and publishes the counts as metric series. The programs count only: they drop no packet and they change none. Enable traffic-usage accounting. The default false attaches nothing and starts no poll loop. Set it true and the config also needs one enabled interface or more under interfaces. Without one, the commit is refused and the error names the missing interface list. An accounting that would report nothing never reaches the kernel. Interfaces to account on. Ze accounts on the interfaces listed here and on no other. An interface with no entry is not accounted, and an entry whose enabled leaf is false is dropped before the attach. With usage enabled and this list empty, the commit is refused. Per-interface traffic-usage accounting. The entry names one interface and can override three leaves of the usage container: track-ip, stale-timeout and max-entries. What the entry does not set, it takes from the leaf of the same name under usage. An entry with a name and no body is accounted with every global value. A change to track-ip or to max-entries makes Ze detach the eBPF programs and attach them again, because both decide the shape of the maps. Account traffic on this interface. The default true accounts on the interface, so an entry with no body needs nothing more. Set it false and Ze drops the entry before it attaches anything. The accounting on that interface stops, and the rest of the list is not touched. To stop the whole feature, use the enabled leaf under usage. Override the global max-entries (per-map LRU capacity) for this interface (inherits when unset). The leaf overrides the max-entries leaf under usage for this interface alone, and an unset leaf takes the global value. The value is the capacity of each LRU map of the interface, so it also sets the memory the interface costs. An effective value of 0 is refused at commit. A change makes Ze attach the eBPF programs again, because a map takes its capacity at creation. Override the global stale-timeout for this interface, in milliseconds. 0 disables the cleanup for this interface. When the leaf is unset, this interface inherits the global stale-timeout. Override the global track-ip for this interface (inherits the global value when unset). The leaf overrides the track-ip leaf under usage for this interface alone, and an unset leaf takes the global value. True adds two more LRU maps to this interface, one for ingress and one for egress, keyed by IPv4 address. A change makes Ze attach the eBPF programs again, because the map set changes. Map poll interval in milliseconds (100ms..1h). One poll loop reads every map of every accounted interface at this period, so the value sets how fresh a metric series is. The default 1000 reads once a second. A value outside 100 milliseconds to 1 hour is refused at commit. The eBPF programs count at line rate whatever this value is, so a longer interval loses no bytes. Per-map LRU capacity; least-recently-used entries are evicted beyond this, keeping top talkers. The value is the capacity of each LRU map, and an interface takes it unless its own max-entries leaf overrides it. Ze creates two maps for each accounted interface, and two more where track-ip is true, so the value sets the memory the accounting costs. Beyond the capacity the kernel evicts the least recently used entry, which keeps the top talkers and loses the quiet ones. Remove a metric series unseen within this many milliseconds; 0 disables cleanup. Ze removes a metric series it has not seen within this time, which stops the series of a talker that left from staying forever. The value 0 disables the cleanup, so every series stays until the plugin stops. An interface can override the value with its own stale-timeout leaf. An interface value that is not 0 and less than 1 second is refused at commit. Account bytes per IPv4 address as well as per interface. The address is the source address on ingress and the destination address on egress. The default is false, which limits the number of metric series.

title: vpn
text: vpn ipsec cookie-threshold uint32 esp-group <name> lifetime uint32 pfs enumeration proposal <number> encryption encryption-algo hash hash-algo ike-group <name> close-action enumeration dead-peer-detection action enumeration interval uint16 timeout uint16 key-exchange enumeration lifetime uint32 proposal <number> dh-group uint8 encryption encryption-algo hash hash-algo interface string policy <name> action enumeration direction enumeration local port union prefix ip-prefix order uint32 protocol uint8 remote port union prefix ip-prefix remote-access authentication mode enumeration x509 ca-certificate string certificate string eap-user <name> certificate string password string esp-group string ike-group string pool <name> dns string domain string range string range6 string site-to-site peer <name> authentication ca-certificate string certificate string certificate-count uint8 certificate-status-request boolean certificate-url string certificate-url-allow ip-prefix hash-and-url boolean local-id string mode enumeration pre-shared-secret string pre-shared-secret-encoding enumeration remote-id string remote-id-type enumeration session-resumption boolean x509 ca-certificate string certificate string connection-type enumeration esp-group string ike-group string local-address string mode enumeration nat-traversal enumeration policy-priority uint32 remote-address string traffic-selector <number> local port union prefix ip-prefix protocol uint8 remote port union prefix ip-prefix transport-required boolean vti bind string unmatched enumeration VPN subsystems. Ze declares one subsystem under it today, which is ipsec. That subsystem holds the ESP groups, the IKE groups and the site-to-site peers. IPsec VPN configuration. Ze speaks IKEv2 (RFC 7296) and installs each negotiated Child SA into the Linux XFRM stack. A peer references one ESP group and one IKE group, and those two carry the algorithms and the timers of the tunnel. Number of half-open IKE SAs tolerated before a COOKIE challenge. Number of half-open IKE SAs tolerated before an inbound IKE_SA_INIT must answer a COOKIE challenge. RFC 7296 Section 2.6 makes the challenge the answer to state and CPU exhaustion from forged source addresses. The default of 0 challenges every inbound initiation, which costs one extra round trip and stops a single spoofed datagram taking a peer's only half-open handshake slot. Raise it to tolerate that many half-open handshakes before challenging. ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) group. The group carries the ESP proposals a peer offers for its Child SAs and the lifetime those SAs run under. A group MUST hold at least one proposal, and commit refuses an empty one. One group holds at most 255 proposals. SA lifetime in seconds. 0 disables expiry. The Child SA rekey trigger sits ahead of the lifetime by the larger of a random 10 percent and one retransmit budget. That lead is capped at half the lifetime. RFC 7296 Section 2.8 states the rule. 'When the lifetime of a Security Association expires, the Security Association MUST NOT be used.' Ze therefore tears the SA down at that point, even when a rekey is still in flight. The value 0 starts no rekey and no expiry. Perfect Forward Secrecy for Child SA rekeying. With enable, Ze puts a KEi payload in the CREATE_CHILD_SA request, and the replacement Child SA is keyed from a fresh Diffie-Hellman secret. With disable, Ze sends no KEi, and the replacement is keyed from SK_d alone, so one leaked SK_d reads every replacement Child SA. RFC 7296 Section 2.17 gives both KEYMAT forms. An ESP proposal carries no Diffie-Hellman group of its own, so Ze offers the group the IKE SA already negotiated. The default is enable, and Ze refuses a response that disagrees with what its request carried. ESP proposal, where a lower number is a higher priority. ESP proposal. Lower number = higher priority. One group offers at most 255 proposals, because RFC 7296 Section 3.3.1 numbers them in one octet. Encryption algorithm. No build carries a transform for chacha20poly1305 or 3des, so a proposal that names one is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement. Integrity algorithm. Integrity algorithm. It is required beside a non-AEAD cipher, and refused beside an AEAD cipher. RFC 7296 Section 3.3 gives an AEAD cipher its own integrity, so an ESP proposal offers the integrity transform NONE. An ESP proposal carries no PRF transform, so this leaf never names one. No build carries a transform for sha1, so a proposal that names it is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement. IKE (Internet Key Exchange) group. The group carries the IKE proposals, the IKE SA lifetime and the Dead Peer Detection timers. A group MUST hold at least one proposal, and commit refuses an empty one. One group holds at most 255 proposals. Action when peer closes the IKE SA. The default is none. The parser stores the value and no other code reads it, so none, start and restart leave the daemon with the same behavior. A session whose IKE SA the peer deletes tears its Child SA down and reconnects on a growing backoff. The session loop does this after every failure. Dead Peer Detection (DPD) settings (RFC 3706). The timers run whether or not this container is present. A peer with no DPD block probes every 30 seconds and waits 120 seconds for the answer. The probe is an empty INFORMATIONAL request, which is the liveness check of RFC 7296 Sections 1.4 and 2.4. Action when DPD detects a dead peer. The default is hold. One log line reads the value when the peer is declared dead, and no other code reads it. The three values restart, hold and clear leave the same behavior. Ze deletes the Child SA, ends the session, and reconnects on a growing backoff. DPD probe interval in seconds. Ze sends the next probe this long after the last one, and it sends none while a probe is outstanding. The default is 30 seconds. DPD timeout in seconds before declaring peer dead. The value bounds the whole liveness budget, so it covers the first probe and every repeat of it. RFC 7296 Section 2.4 allows the verdict only when 'repeated attempts to contact it have gone unanswered for a timeout period'. Ze repeats the probe on a growing backoff inside the budget and tears the SA down when the budget runs out. The default is 120 seconds. IKE protocol version. The default is ikev2 and the engine writes major version 2 into every header it sends. The parser stores the value and no other code reads it, so a group that names ikev1 commits and still runs IKEv2. IKE SA lifetime in seconds, where 0 starts no rekey. Ze rekeys the IKE SA before the lifetime runs out, on the trigger the ESP group lifetime describes. It also rekeys the SA as the message id space nears its ceiling. RFC 7296 Section 2.2 requires that. 'In the unlikely event that Message IDs grow too large to fit in 32 bits, the IKE SA MUST be closed or rekeyed.' The value 0 starts no rekey, so the SA runs until the peer or the operator ends it. IKE proposal, where a lower number is a higher priority. IKE proposal. Lower number = higher priority. One group offers at most 255 proposals, because RFC 7296 Section 3.3.1 numbers them in one octet. Diffie-Hellman group number (RFC 7296 Section 3.3.2). The number is Transform Type 4 of RFC 7296 Section 3.3.2. That section lists the values current at publication, up to 18, and sends the reader to the IANA registry for later ones. Ze takes 1 to 31 and refuses a group this build carries no transform for. The refusal lists the numbers the build does carry, which stops the reserved Transform ID 0 reaching the wire. Encryption algorithm. No build carries a transform for chacha20poly1305 or 3des, so a proposal that names one is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement. PRF and integrity algorithm. It is required beside every cipher, and an AEAD cipher is no exception. RFC 7296 Section 3.3.3 makes the PRF a mandatory transform for an IKE proposal, and this leaf names it. An ESP proposal reads the same leaf as integrity alone, and refuses it beside an AEAD cipher. No build carries a transform for sha1, so a proposal that names it is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement. WAN interface for IPsec traffic. Commit refuses a name no interface on the host carries. The first IPv4 address of the interface fills the local-address of every peer that names none. The IKE socket on port 500 binds there. The NAT-T socket on port 4500 also binds there unless live XFRM migration is available, when it listens on the wildcard and selects each SA's source address explicitly. A reload whose interface holds no IPv4 address is refused, and the same case at startup runs and writes a warning. Operator-authored Security Policy Database entry. An entry of the Security Policy Database that Ze installs directly, rather than one a Child SA negotiation produces. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 gives the database three dispositions: 'PROTECT, BYPASS, or DISCARD'. A peer under site-to-site produces the PROTECT entries, because those name a transform and a peer to negotiate it with. The other two name neither, so they are written here: BYPASS lets traffic cross the IPsec boundary in the clear, and DISCARD stops it at the boundary. Section 7.4 makes the discard disposition an obligation: 'All implementations MUST support DISCARDing of fragments using the normal SPD packet classification mechanisms.' This list is the management interface that Section 4.4.1 requires for it. Ze installs every entry when the configuration is applied and removes it when the entry leaves the configuration. An entry needs no peer, no key and no negotiation, so it is in force whether or not any tunnel is up. What the entry does with the traffic its selector matches. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 defines bypass as 'to allow the packet to pass without IPsec protection' and discard as 'to discard the traffic, i.e., not to let the traffic traverse the IPsec boundary'. There is no protect here on purpose. A protect entry names an ESP transform, a mode and a peer to negotiate keys with, and those live under site-to-site peer. Offering the word in both places would put one concept in two grammars. The leaf is mandatory rather than defaulted. A defaulted disposition is the one field of this entry whose wrong value is silent: a bypass written where a discard was meant passes exactly the traffic the operator wrote the entry to stop. Which side of the boundary the entry acts on. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 splits the database by direction: SPD-O holds the outbound bypass and discard entries and SPD-I holds the inbound ones. A policy is one-way, so a Ze entry is one-way too. both installs the mirrored pair: the outbound entry keeps local and remote as written, and the inbound entry swaps them, because the local side of a flow is the DESTINATION of an inbound packet. It is the default because a one-way discard leaves the return traffic crossing the boundary, which almost never expresses what the operator meant. The local side of the selector. Local is Ze's own side of the IPsec boundary. It is the source of an outbound packet and the destination of an inbound one, which is the swap direction both performs. Local port of the selector. One exact port, or any for every port. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1.1 defines the selector as a list of ranges; the kernel selector Ze programs carries a port and a mask, which expresses every port or one exact port and no range between them. A range is refused rather than widened to any, because widening would bypass or discard traffic the operator did not name. Local traffic the entry matches. The value is a CIDR prefix and Ze installs it as the local selector of the policy. Use 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 for every address. The two prefixes of one entry MUST share an address family, and commit refuses a mixed pair because a kernel selector carries one family. Rank of this entry, lowest searched fi

title: vpp
text: vpp api-socket string cpu main-core uint8 poll-sleep string worker-cores string workers uint8 dpdk interface <pci-address> name string rx-queues uint8 tx-queues uint8 enabled boolean external boolean lcp auto-subint boolean enabled boolean netns string sync boolean memory buffers uint32 hugepage-size enumeration main-heap string plugins wireguard boolean stats poll-interval uint16 segment-size string socket-path string VPP data plane configuration. Ze reads this subtree at startup and writes /etc/vpp/startup.conf from it, then starts /usr/bin/vpp. A change committed later logs "config reload requires daemon restart to take effect" and does not reach VPP until the daemon restarts. The enabled leaf is false by default, so every other leaf here changes nothing until you set it to true. GoVPP binary API Unix socket path. Ze writes this path into the socksvr section of startup.conf and then connects to it through GoVPP. The path MUST be absolute, MUST NOT contain "..", and MUST be 108 characters or less, which is the Unix socket path limit. Under external true Ze writes no startup.conf, so this leaf is the only setting Ze needs to reach a VPP process another supervisor started. Ze retries the connection 10 times, one second apart, inside a 30-second budget. VPP CPU pinning configuration. These leaves write the cpu section of startup.conf, and the main-core leaf pins the VPP main thread. The workers leaf asks for a count, and Ze takes those cores from the set the kernel isolated, which it reads from /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated. The worker-cores leaf names the cores instead, and it MUST NOT be set beside workers. The poll-sleep leaf sits here for the operator, and Ze emits it in the unix section, because that is where VPP reads poll-sleep-usec. Omit every leaf to let VPP place its own threads, and Ze checks a placement leaf you set at commit. Ze refuses a core the host does not hold, a worker core that is also main-core, and a worker count the host cannot satisfy. CPU core for VPP main thread. Omit for automatic assignment. Ze writes this core number into the cpu section of startup.conf as main-core. The core is excluded from the worker set, so the main thread and a worker never share a CPU. Omit the leaf and VPP picks the main core itself, and Ze still counts the worker list from core 1. A core the host does not hold online is refused at commit. Fixed sleep between VPP main-loop polls, in whole milliseconds. Fixed sleep between VPP main-loop polls, expressed in whole milliseconds, which is the only accepted unit, for example 10ms. Ze emits it as unix { poll-sleep-usec N } in startup.conf, where 1ms is 1000 microseconds. Omit the leaf for VPP's default, where the workers busy-poll at 100% CPU with no sleep, and the latency is lowest. Set a non-zero value up to 100ms on a shared or dev host, to trade latency for idle CPU. An explicit 0ms is emitted and equals the default. Explicit CPU core list for the VPP worker threads. Ze writes these cores into the corelist-workers line of the cpu section in startup.conf, and writes no line when neither leaf is set. The syntax is the one the kernel uses for isolcpus: single cores, ranges, or both, as in 2-4 or 2,4,6. Set this leaf when the isolated set holds cores to keep for something else, and omit it to derive the cores from workers. It MUST NOT be set beside workers, because the two are separate answers to the same question, and Ze refuses a config that carries both. A core the host does not hold online, a core that is also main-core, and a core listed twice are each refused at commit. Cores outside the kernel's isolated set are accepted, and the vpp-cpu-isolation doctor check reports them. Number of VPP worker threads. Omit for automatic (one per available core). Ze turns this count into the corelist-workers line of the cpu section in startup.conf, and the worker-cores leaf names those cores instead. Ze takes the cores from the set the kernel isolated at boot, lowest first, with main-core excluded. Isolated 2-4 with main-core 2 and workers 2 therefore emits corelist-workers 3-4. When the kernel isolated no core, the list is contiguous and starts one core after main-core, so 4 workers with main-core 1 emits corelist-workers 2-5. The vpp-cpu-isolation doctor check then reports that the workers share their CPUs with Linux. A count the host cannot satisfy is refused at commit, and a value of 0 emits no line, which is what an absent leaf does. DPDK NIC configuration. Every NIC listed here is unbound from its kernel driver and bound to vfio-pci before VPP starts, so Linux loses the interface. Ze saves the original driver name and rebinds it when the daemon stops. Under external true Ze binds nothing, because the external supervisor owns that step. An empty list emits no dpdk section in startup.conf. DPDK-managed network interface. The list key is the PCI address, so this list holds one entry for each NIC. Ze loads the vfio, vfio_pci and vfio_iommu_type1 kernel modules, then binds each listed address to vfio-pci. A bind failure on one NIC unbinds every NIC Ze bound in the same pass, and VPP does not start. Short interface name (e.g. xe0, e1). Used in ze CLI and config. Ze writes this name into the dev entry of the dpdk section in startup.conf, so VPP calls the interface by it. The name is 1 to 15 characters of letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot, and a hyphen or a dot MUST NOT come first. Omit the leaf and Ze writes no name line, so VPP picks the interface name itself. Number of receive queues. Omit for VPP default. Ze writes this count into the dev entry of the dpdk section as num-rx-queues. An explicit 0 is written out, so it is not the same as an absent leaf. Omit the leaf and the line is absent, which leaves VPP on its own default. Ze does not compare the count against the queues the NIC holds. Number of transmit queues. Omit for VPP default. Ze writes this count into the dev entry of the dpdk section as num-tx-queues. An explicit 0 is written out, so it is not the same as an absent leaf. Omit the leaf and the line is absent, which leaves VPP on its own default. Ze does not compare the count against the queues the NIC holds. Enable VPP integration, so Ze manages the VPP lifecycle. Enable VPP integration. When this leaf is true, Ze manages the VPP lifecycle. Ze generates startup.conf, binds the DPDK NICs, starts the VPP process, and connects through GoVPP. Let an external supervisor own the VPP process, false by default. When this leaf is true, Ze does not exec or supervise the VPP process, generate startup.conf, or bind DPDK NICs. The external supervisor owns all of that. Ze only connects through GoVPP to api-socket. Use this leaf for systemd-managed VPP, for a container sidecar deployment, or for the `le test vpp` stub harness. The default is false, where Ze owns the VPP lifecycle. Linux Control Plane plugin settings. Linux Control Plane plugin. The plugin creates TAP mirrors in Linux for VPP interfaces. A routing daemon such as ze BGP can then use Linux TCP on a VPP-managed NIC. Auto-create sub-TAPs for dot1q/QinQ sub-interfaces. When this leaf is true, Ze writes lcp-auto-subint into the linux-cp section of startup.conf. A dot1q or QinQ sub-interface created in VPP then gets its own Linux sub-TAP. When it is false, Ze omits the line, so a sub-interface has no mirror in Linux and only its parent interface does. The default is true, and lcp enabled MUST also be true before Ze writes the line. Enable LCP plugin in VPP. When this leaf is true, Ze enables linux_cp_plugin.so and linux_nl_plugin.so in startup.conf, and writes the linux-cp and linux-nl sections. When it is false, no other lcp leaf reaches startup.conf and the netns leaf is not validated. The default is true. LCP gives each VPP interface a TAP mirror in Linux, so a routing daemon binds an ordinary Linux socket. Network namespace for LCP TAP interfaces. Routing daemons run in this namespace. Ze writes this name into the linux-cp section of startup.conf as default netns. VPP then creates the TAP mirrors under /var/run/netns/NAME. An EMPTY value is valid, and Ze then omits the line. It is the one value that leaves the TAPs in the namespace Ze runs in. An absent leaf is not the same as an empty one, because Ze seeds the default "dataplane" when the leaf is absent. With any name, Ze binds BGP in its own namespace and cannot bind on an LCP TAP address, which the doctor check vpp-lcp-netns reports. A name with a path separator, a space or an unprintable character is refused at commit. VPP truncates a name at a space, so the namespace it then opens under /var/run/netns/ does not exist. Sync VPP state changes (link, MTU, IP) to Linux TAP mirrors. When this leaf is true, Ze writes lcp-sync into the linux-cp section of startup.conf. A link, MTU or address change made in VPP then reaches the Linux TAP mirror. When it is false, Ze omits the line and the two sides drift apart. The default is true, and lcp enabled MUST also be true before Ze writes the line. VPP memory and buffer configuration. These three leaves decide how much hugepage memory VPP asks the host for. The ze doctor check adds the main heap, the buffer memory and the stats segment together. It warns when the host reserved less hugepage memory than that sum. The hugepage-size leaf decides which page size VPP asks for, and it also governs the stats segment. Number of packet buffers per NUMA node. 128000 is proven for full DFZ at 10G. Ze writes this count into the buffers section of startup.conf as buffers-per-numa, beside a fixed default data-size of 2048 bytes. The packet data alone costs the count multiplied by 2048 bytes on each NUMA node, so the default 128000 needs 250 MiB plus buffer metadata and alignment. A value of 0 is refused at commit with "vpp: memory buffers must be > 0". Hugepage size for VPP buffers. The two accepted values are 2M and 1G. For 1G Ze writes page-size 1G into both the buffers section and the statseg section of startup.conf. For 2M Ze writes page-size default-hugepage instead, which takes whatever the kernel holds as its default hugepage size. The ze doctor check warns when you select 1G on an amd64 CPU with no pdpe1gb flag, because the kernel then reserves no 1G page. VPP main heap size (e.g. 512M, 1G, 1536M). Production with full DFZ: 1536M. Ze writes this size into the memory section of startup.conf as main-heap-size. The value MUST be digits followed by M or G, so 1536M is accepted and 1.5G is refused at commit. The ze doctor check counts this size toward the hugepage memory it expects the host to have reserved. Optional VPP plugins to load. Optional VPP plugin enablement. startup.conf uses 'plugin default { disable }', so Ze loads only the always-on plugins and the plugins toggled on here. The always-on plugins are dpdk, plus linux-cp when lcp is enabled. Load wireguard_plugin.so for the vpp interface backend. Load wireguard_plugin.so so the vpp interface backend can program WireGuard tunnels. The tunnels are configured as interface wireguard under backend vpp. VPP stats segment configuration. The stats segment is the shared memory area VPP writes its counters into. Ze connects to it separately from the binary API and reads it for Prometheus metrics, at the interval poll-interval sets. A failed stats connection logs "vpp: stats connection failed, telemetry disabled" and leaves the rest of the VPP integration running. Stats polling interval in seconds. Stats polling interval in seconds. The interval controls how often Ze reads VPP's stats segment for Prometheus metrics. Stats segment shared memory size. Ze writes this size into the statseg section of startup.conf as size. The value MUST be digits followed by M or G, so 512M and 1G are accepted and 512MB is refused at commit. The page size of the segment comes from memory hugepage-size and not from this leaf. The ze doctor check counts this size toward the hugepage memory it expects the host to have reserved. title: Dependencies
text: Dependencies Ze is Go, and Go code leans on packages. 52 direct dependencies, read straight from go.mod so the list and versions can't drift -- each one with a plain-English reason it's there, grounded in where it's actually imported, not its own pitch. Terminal, Web & SSH Interfaces (9) Module Version Why we use it --- --- --- charm.land/bubbletea/v2 v2.0.9 The Elm-style TUI framework driving Ze's interactive CLI: config editor, dashboard, monitor, ping and traceroute views, run per SSH session. charm.land/bubbles/v2 v2.2.1 Pre-built TUI widgets (text input, viewport) for the CLI's interactive screens. charm.land/lipgloss/v2 v2.0.6 Styling and layout for the CLI's colors, borders, and widths. charm.land/wish/v2 v2.0.3 SSH server middleware that wires each incoming session to run the CLI's Bubbletea program. charm.land/ssh v0.4.3 SSH session and public-key types that the wish server and the CLI's key-based auth build on. github.com/a-h/templ v0.3.1020 Compiles the typed server-rendered components used by Ze's web configuration interface and BGP looking glass into Go. github.com/charmbracelet/colorprofile v0.4.3 Forces a deterministic color profile in render tests, so CLI screenshot/layout tests don't depend on the terminal running them. github.com/muesli/reflow v0.3.0 ANSI-aware text width calculation, so the CLI's prompt and status bar line up correctly despite embedded color codes. github.com/creack/pty v1.1.24 Opens a pseudo-terminal in a Linux integration test that exercises serial console handling. Networking & Protocols (6) Module Version Why we use it --- --- --- github.com/miekg/dns v1.1.73 DNS message parsing and serving underneath Ze's DNS server engine, the AS112 blackhole plugin, and GeoDNS. It's the library underpinning CoreDNS. github.com/insomniacslk/dhcp v0.0.0-20260719225207-c76316d4aa82 DHCPv4/DHCPv6 client used for interface lease handling and the installer's disk-provisioning DHCP client. github.com/beevik/ntp v1.5.0 NTP client queries used by the ntp plugin. golang.zx2c4.com/wireguard/wgctrl v0.0.0-20241231184526-a9ab2273dd10 Creates and configures WireGuard interfaces and peers from the interface netlink backend. github.com/mdlayher/packet v1.1.2 Raw AF PACKET sockets behind the diag capture CLI command. github.com/packetcap/go-pcap v0.0.0-20251215121130-f2cf9f991e7c Only its filter subpackage: parses tcpdump/BPF-style filter expressions for diag capture . Packet capture itself goes through mdlayher/packet instead. Linux Kernel Interfaces (7) Module Version Why we use it --- --- --- github.com/vishvananda/netlink v1.3.1 The main library for configuring the Linux network stack: links, addresses, routes, neighbors, bridges, VLANs, tunnels, IPsec, QoS. Used across interfaces, traffic, FIB, OSPF, ISIS, and MPLS. github.com/vishvananda/netns v0.0.5 Linux network-namespace handles, used alongside netlink for namespace-scoped route watching. github.com/google/nftables v0.3.0 Programs the kernel's nftables firewall (tables, chains, rules, sets) over netlink. github.com/mdlayher/netlink v1.11.2 Low-level generic netlink sockets, used to flush conntrack flow entries for flow export. github.com/mdlayher/genetlink v1.4.0 Generic netlink family dialing, used to attach to the kernel's psample subsystem for sampled flow export. github.com/cilium/ebpf v0.22.0 Assembles and attaches eBPF programs in pure Go, no clang or libbpf needed, to count traffic for the trafficusage plugin. filippo.io/mlockexe v1.0.0 Locks the running ze executable's own file-backed pages in memory with mlock2(2) and MLOCK ONFAULT, so the kernel cannot evict the daemon's text under memory pressure. A router short of memory reclaims page cache, and the running daemon IS page cache: without the lock it waits on the disk holding its own binary at the moment it must keep sessions alive. Routing & Dataplane (2) Module Version Why we use it --- --- --- github.com/gaissmai/bart v0.29.0 Balanced Routing Table, built on Knuth's Allotment Routing Table (ART): the longest-prefix-match structure underneath Ze's RIB store. go.fd.io/govpp v0.13.0 Binary-API client for FD.io VPP, used by the optional VPP dataplane backends for interfaces, firewall, traffic, FIB, and IKE. Config, RPC & Telemetry (5) Module Version Why we use it --- --- --- github.com/openconfig/goyang v1.6.3 Parses and validates the YANG module definitions behind Ze's config schema, CLI completion, and validation engine. github.com/openconfig/gnmi v0.14.1 Generated gNMI protobuf/gRPC types that Ze's gNMI server implements for Get/Set/Subscribe/Capabilities. google.golang.org/grpc v1.83.2 Backs Ze's gRPC servers: gNMI and Ze's own management API. google.golang.org/protobuf v1.36.12 Runtime support for the generated protobuf message types behind Ze's gRPC API. google.golang.org/grpc/cmd/protoc-gen-go-grpc v1.6.2 Build-time only: the protoc plugin used to regenerate the gRPC API's Go bindings from ze.proto. Observability (5) Module Version Why we use it --- --- --- github.com/prometheus/client golang v1.24.1 Ze's internal metrics backend: counters, gauges, and histograms against a private registry. github.com/prometheus/client model v0.6.2 The metric sample types the L2TP subscriber tests and the BGP interop lab read a gauge's current value through. github.com/prometheus/common v0.70.1 Reads the Prometheus text exposition format back: the IPsec interop test parses Ze's own metrics answer and compares the gauges against the kernel. github.com/prometheus/procfs v0.22.0 Parses Linux /proc for the telemetry collector: CPU, memory, network device and socket stats, conntrack, softnet. github.com/sirupsen/logrus v1.10.2 Only to satisfy GoVPP's logging interface, bridged into Ze's own slog logger via a hook. Not used as Ze's own logger. title: Configuration Syntax Changes
text: Configuration Syntax Changes Ze has not shipped a stable configuration release yet. There is no public deprecation lifecycle for old config versions, and Ze does not promise a numbered generation ladder for config syntax. Config compatibility is date-based. A config file records the schema stamp that wrote it, and recovery chooses the newest rollback file that the running binary can parse. For pre-release files or old examples, ze config migrate converts known older shapes to the syntax expected by the current tree. Compatibility rules Case What Ze does ------ -------------- Current config ze config validate <file checks it directly. Older pre-release Ze syntax ze config migrate applies named transforms, then emits current syntax. ExaBGP-shaped syntax The migrator converts supported shapes and reports unsupported extensions. Newer schema stamp after downgrade Startup tries rollback files newest-first and writes back the first one this binary can parse. The transform names are descriptive implementation names, not public config version numbers. Use ze config migrate --list to see the current list in the binary you are running. Older shapes the migrator recognizes Root-level neighbor Older examples sometimes used root-level neighbor blocks: neighbor 192.0.2.1 { local-as 65000; peer-as 65001; } Current native config puts BGP under bgp {} and separates transport from BGP session state: bgp { session { asn { local 65000; } } peer upstream1 { connection { remote { ip 192.0.2.1; } } session { asn { remote 65001; } } } } Root-level peer globs Older configs could use root-level peer globs for shared defaults: peer { hold-time 90; } Current config uses named groups and concrete peers: bgp { group default { timer { receive-hold-time 90; } peer upstream1 { connection { remote { ip 192.0.2.1; } } session { asn { remote 65001; } } } } } template { neighbor } Older template neighbors became peer groups: template { neighbor ibgp-rs { peer-as 65000; } } Current config expresses the same default as a BGP group: bgp { group ibgp-rs { session { asn { remote 65000; } } } } Unsupported ExaBGP extensions ze exabgp migrate translates the capability keywords Ze has a session setting for, and WARNS about every other keyword the block holds. The warning goes to stderr, names the peer and names each keyword in one line. The migrated session negotiates less than the ExaBGP config asked for, so read the warnings before you deploy the output. The set is derived, not listed: migrateCapability declares the keywords it translates ( route-refresh , extended-message , link-local-nexthop , asn4 , graceful-restart , software-version , add-path ), and anything else in the block reaches the warning. A keyword ExaBGP adds later is therefore reported without an edit here. Syntax Result -------- -------- capability { multi-session; } Warns: peer <name : the capability block asks for "multi-session", which ze exabgp migrate does not translate, so the migrated config does not ask for it capability { aigp enable; } Same warning, naming aigp . Ze's AIGP codec is always on and has no per-peer switch, so there is no setting to translate the keyword into Several in one peer One warning names them all, in the order the block declares them operational { ... } under an ExaBGP neighbor ze exabgp migrate stops at the parser: line N: unknown field in neighbor: operational capability { multi-session; } in Ze syntax ze config migrate stops at the parser: line N: unknown field in capability: multi-session operational { ... } under a peer, in Ze syntax ze config migrate stops at the parser: line N: unknown field in peer: operational The capability block is the only place a warning replaces a refusal. An operational { ... } block, in either syntax, is a parse error: the grammar has no such field, so there is nothing to leave out. Two of the keywords are worth knowing by name, because each comes from an IETF draft that expired without becoming an RFC. Extension Draft Expired Codepoint ----------- ------- --------- ----------- multi-session draft-ietf-idr-bgp-multisession-07 2013-03-16 Section 4 assigns capability code 68 operational draft-ietf-idr-operational-message-00 2012-09-01 Section 9 requests a capability code and a BGP message type from IANA. Neither was allocated operational therefore has no assigned value to put on the wire. ExaBGP fills both with private values of its own, capability 0xB9 and message type 0x06 . Ze does not copy a private codepoint. Commands Check whether a file already matches the current binary ze config validate config.conf Preview conversion without writing a new file ze config migrate --dry-run config.conf Convert to stdout ze config migrate config.conf Convert to a new file ze config migrate -o config-current.conf config.conf List transforms in this binary ze config migrate --list See Configuration Migration for command details.

title: Ze Features
text: Ze Features Ze is an open-source configuration and protocol engine written in Go. The network operating system built on it runs on any Linux or as a gokrazy appliance. Status values: Supported means implemented and covered in the normal release evidence for this pre-release; Experimental means implemented but still needs deployment evidence or hardening before production claims; Partial means a named subset is not implemented or not proven; Stub-backed means external dependency evidence currently comes from a stub harness; Rejected means unsupported by design; Future means planned but not shipped. Feature Status Description --------- -------- ------------- BGP Protocol Supported 23 address families, 14 capabilities, 15 path attributes. bgp update-delay max-delay <seconds holds the first advertisement of a speaker that has just started until every configured peer has sent its End-of-RIB marker, until an optional establish-wait expires, or until max-delay expires, so a neighbor receives one settled route set instead of an initial set followed by corrections; RFC 4724 Section 4.1 prescribes the same deferral for a restarting speaker and requires the configurable upper bound. show bgp update-delay reports whether the speaker is holding and what it waits for. The whole BGP subsystem is compile-out-able with the ze bgp build tag. The default feature list includes it, while bare ze core builds drop internal/component/bgp entirely -- engine, wire codec, RIB, and every BGP plugin -- plus flowspec-firewall , which translates BGP-delivered flowspec routes and is meaningless without it. Both composition roots are gated (the generated all ze bgp.go , and the package main root, which splits into cmd/ze/dispatch bgp.go for the CLI registration under ze core && ze bgp and cmd/ze/infra bgp.go for the always-on seams under ze bgp alone), and a bgp {} config block is rejected as an unknown field rather than silently ignored. A BGP-less daemon still runs OSPF, IS-IS, static routes, the FIB, MRT recording, and flow export: the route-action vocabulary, the BGP message-type codes, and the best-path-change event contract those consumers share live in always-on internal/core/bgp/ leaves, and the places always-on code used to call into the engine are inversion-of-control seams the engine fills from its own init() : internal/component/config/infra carries four of them ( ze config dump/diff/validate resolution, BGP peer validation, roleless-peer reporting, and the graceful-restart marker), and the MRT RIB dump provider is a fifth. le chaos run and le perf drive an in-process reactor and force ze bgp on. Within a ze bgp build the BMP monitoring plugin (RFC 7854/8671/9069) is independently compile-out-able with the ze bmp build tag: it is a dependent gate. BMP imports the engine, so all ze bmp.go is generated with //go:build ze bgp && ze bmp , and a ze bmp -without- ze bgp build links neither BMP nor the engine. Configuration Partial YANG-modeled config with prefix limits, update groups, session resilience, duplicate list-key rejection, side-effect-free in-process plugin verifiers for static/API/CLI validation, and transactional commits using active/candidate/rollback pointers. Live external plugin OnConfigVerify callbacks run only in daemon reload/commit transactions. Persistent storage Experimental One live database/ tree holds checksummed keys, credentials, runtime state, and per-config version pointers. Config history is content-addressed: each version's bytes are stored once under their SHA-256, and every read verifies the hash. One process owns writes; read-only inspection remains available. Explicit config files remain authoritative on every explicit-file start. Daemon commits update the file and history through a recoverable publication intent. ZeFS blobs remain explicit offline artifacts and appliance seeds. Backup and restore Experimental ze data backup <file [spare <n ] copies every key of the live store to one new 0600 blob artifact under the write lock, so a commit is in the backup whole or not at all. ze data restore <file config [name <source-name ] commits one config from a verified artifact as a new version of this device's config and leaves credentials, identity and history unchanged. ze data restore <file full replaces the whole tree, moves the previous tree to database.replaced-<stamp , and records a durable intent, so an interrupted restore is refused by every opener until the same command finishes it. Both verbs are offline; while a daemon owns the store, request data backup path <file and request data restore path <file config run over SSH, and a restored config becomes active only when the reload accepts it. ze init --from <path-or-url [--sha256 <hex ] creates a store from a blob, with the digest checked before a key is written. ze config edit --backup <artifact edits a config inside a backup with no daemon. Deactivate / Activate Supported Junos-style inactive: prefix on any node (leaf, container, list entry, leaf-list value); kept in file, skipped at apply. CLI: ze config deactivate/activate <file <path . TUI: deactivate <path / activate <path . Engine-level, no schema annotation required. Environment Variables Supported Ze-native env surface: ze.user , ze.pid.file , ze.pprof , ze.bgp.openwait , ze.bgp.announce.delay , ze.cli.format ; ExaBGP-compat env keys retired 2026-04 Outbound source-address Supported Optional source-address local-IP binding for outbound service connections: BMP collector, RPKI/RTR cache, flow-export (UDP), IRR whois, and the managed hub TLS client; LDP binds its transport-address as the session source (RFC 5036). Unset = OS-selected source (unchanged). Shared network.RealDialer applies the bind for TCP/TLS; flow-export binds the UDP socket. See Outbound Source Address. CLI Default Output Format Supported Configurable default output format via environment { cli { format { default text; } } } . Supported values: text (default), table, json, yaml, ndjson. Session override via set cli format <value in operational mode. Explicit pipe operators ( \ json , \ table , etc.) always win over the configured default, and over the --format flag of ze cli -c . Interfaces Experimental Linux interface management via netlink: ethernet, dummy, veth, bridge, loopback, VLAN (with 802.1p ingress/egress QoS maps translating PCP to internal priority and back, and named class-of-service profiles via the cos plugin with interface-level inheritance and per-unit override/opt-out; dynamic per-subscriber CoS via RADIUS Filter-Id "cos:\<name\ " or vendor-specific attributes (Cisco-AVPair, Juniper ERX, Nokia, Huawei) applied on session-up with mid-session CoA changes and session-down revert; MikroTik Mikrotik-Rate-Limit VSA for shaper rate extraction ), 9 tunnel kinds (GRE, GRETAP, IP6GRE, IP6GRETAP, IPIP, SIT, IP6TNL, IPIP6, VXLAN with a 24-bit VNI over UDP 4789 per RFC 7348), each carrying an outer-header TTL of 64 when the config names none, so an encapsulated packet survives a multi-hop underlay; ttl 0 still asks the kernel to inherit the inner packet's TTL, and the default reaches netlink-backed tunnels only, because the VPP tunnel calls carry no TTL field, so a commit that names a ttl on a vpp-backed tunnel is refused by path rather than accepted and dropped , and WireGuard (declarative peers with $9$ -encoded keys); DHCP (config-driven, routes, DNS, NTP discovery), NTP client (clock sync, RTC, time persistence, max-step safety cap), monitoring, migration, mirroring, per-interface offload and steering (GRO, GSO, SG, TSO, LRO, hw-tc-offload via kernel ethtool ioctl; RPS, RFS via sysfs; boolean three-state: true/false/absent), per-family reverse path filtering ( rpf-check strict\ loose\ disable in ipv4/ipv6 containers, backed by rp filter sysctl on Linux; IPv6 enforcement requires VPP), per-interface rate tracking (1s sampler with show interface rate , monitor interface rate , 12 ze interface Prometheus gauges, web rate columns). Local privileged integration

title: Glossary
text: Glossary Terms used in Ze documentation and operator output. BGP and routing Adj-RIB-In Routes accepted from a peer and retained before or alongside local best-path selection. Ze does not keep every import-rejected route unless a component explicitly records it. Adj-RIB-Out Routes selected and prepared for advertisement to one peer. AFI/SAFI Address Family Identifier and Subsequent Address Family Identifier. Together they identify a BGP family such as IPv4 unicast, EVPN, or FlowSpec. AS path The sequence of autonomous systems a BGP route has traversed. Ze uses it for loop detection, policy, best-path selection, and topology display. BART Balanced Routing Table, the gaissmai/bart library under Ze's prefix-keyed route store. It is Knuth's Allotment Routing Table (ART) laid out as a stride-8 multibit trie. It is unrelated to the Adaptive Radix Tree (Leis et al., 2013), which shares the ART acronym. BGP Role An RFC 9234 relationship such as provider, customer, peer, route server, or route-server client. Roles help detect route leaks and control OTC processing. End-of-RIB A BGP marker indicating that the initial or refreshed update stream for a family is complete. FIB Forwarding Information Base. The routes programmed into a dataplane such as the Linux kernel, VPP, or P4. Loc-RIB The local set of selected routes after protocol and policy processing. NLRI Network Layer Reachability Information. The family-specific route payload carried by BGP. RIB Routing Information Base. A route store used for candidate, accepted, selected, or advertised routing state, depending on context. RPKI Resource Public Key Infrastructure. Ze uses validated ROA data received over RTR to determine whether a route origin is Valid, Invalid, or NotFound. RTR RPKI-to-Router protocol used between a validating cache and a router. Resilience and policy ADD-PATH A BGP capability that allows more than one path for the same prefix to cross a session. Send and receive modes are negotiated per family. Graceful Restart RFC 4724 behaviour that retains stale forwarding state while a BGP speaker restarts and refreshes its routes. Long-Lived Graceful Restart RFC 9494 extension that retains and deprioritises stale routes beyond the ordinary Graceful Restart window. Import filter An ordered policy chain applied to a route received from a peer before it enters eligible local routing state. Export filter An ordered policy chain applied for one destination peer before advertisement. OTC Only-to-Customer, the RFC 9234 path attribute used with BGP Roles to detect and prevent route leaks. Route reflection RFC 4456 distribution of iBGP routes through reflectors and clients, avoiding a full iBGP mesh. Route server A BGP speaker that distributes eligible routes between participants while preserving the participant next hop and applying per-member policy. Ze configuration and operation Active configuration The configuration revision currently applied to the running system. Candidate configuration A proposed configuration revision being edited and validated before commit. Commit The transaction that verifies, applies, and activates a candidate configuration. In route injection, a named commit window groups route operations atomically. Component A Ze subsystem that owns runtime behaviour, configuration, commands, health, metrics, or plugins. Doctor Offline readiness checks run with ze doctor . Findings have structured diagnostic codes that can be inspected with ze explain . Handler A callback registered by a component or plugin for configuration, commands, events, codecs, validation, or lifecycle stages. Plugin A registered Ze extension. Plugins may run in process or as external programs and can own configuration, commands, events, filters, families, services, or dataplane integration. Plugin hub The authenticated transport and dispatch layer used by external plugins and managed components. It is separate from Fleet Management even when configuration shares a surrounding plugin block. ZeFS Ze's blob artifact format ( .zefs ): a seed, a backup, or an import source carrying the same keys as the live database/ store. It is never the live store. Operator surfaces CLI The interactive or one-shot command interface reached over Ze's SSH server. gNMI The OpenConfig gRPC Network Management Interface used for YANG-oriented Capabilities, Get, Set, and Subscribe operations. Looking Glass The public read-only BGP peer, route, search, and AS-path view. It runs separately from the authenticated web workbench. MCP Model Context Protocol. Ze exposes registered commands and structured resources to authorised AI clients through its MCP server. Web workbench The authenticated browser interface for configuration, commands, operational tables, and live state. Testing Functional transcript A .ci scenario that drives real processes, commands, files, HTTP requests, peers, and expected outputs. Interop test A scenario that runs Ze against another real implementation such as FRR, BIRD, GoBGP, strongSwan, xl2tpd, or accel-ppp. Property An invariant checked across a scenario, such as convergence, route isolation, or state consistency. Shrink Reduction of a recorded chaos event sequence to the smallest sequence that still reproduces a failure.

title: RFC Implementation Status
text: RFC Implementation Status This page is Ze's public standards status page. It lists RFCs that Ze implements, partially implements, has deferred, or has explicitly decided not to implement. It is a product support view rather than a formal IETF compliance certificate: Supported means the behavior is implemented and tied to current source anchors; Experimental means implemented but still needs deployment evidence or hardening before production claims; Partial means a named subset is missing, intentionally skipped, or not proven; Unsupported means Ze explicitly does not implement it; Future means tracked but not shipped. Every row below is declared by the RFC's own summary, in the ## Meta table of rfc/short/<stem .md . A row belongs here only when current docs, source code, tests, or learned closure notes tie the RFC to a Ze feature, and a summary that ties to none writes Support - instead. This page is the product view. The per-requirement detail behind it is published at /quality/rfc-compliance/<stem / , one page for every summary under rfc/short/ , naming each requirement, the tests bound to it, the audit verdict a reader recorded, and every gap and untested MUST under its own requirement id. The 36 of 202 summaries (17.8%) with no row on this page are published there too, and the index at /quality/rfc-compliance/ links all of them. How strong the proof behind a row is. Every requirement's evidence is listed in that RFC's own file under rfc/requirements/ , with a kind/tier cell per test link. kind is the layer the test exercises ( unit , functional , editor , interop ); tier is whether anything executes it. verify means it runs in ./le verify current mode full on every push. interop/nightly runs only in the scheduled, advisory evidence-nightly workflow -- so a requirement whose evidence is entirely nightly-tier is marked nightly-only on its row there, and counted in its own column of the coverage rollup in ai/RFC-REQUIREMENTS.md , and a row here backed only by such evidence is not proven on the merge path. A tag in a suite no pipeline runs is refused outright rather than published with a caveat. What on this page a machine checks, and what stays a human judgement. ./le rfc check enforces exactly three properties of the tables below. - Gap-count agreement. A Support remaining cell can spell a number immediately before MUST or SHALL. That number must equal the count of {gap} plus {partial} requirement rows in the same summary. - Disclosure under a {gap} . A summary can privately admit an unmet MUST. Its row here must then say so, in the Status cell or in the Remaining cell. - A support claim rests on something. Two rows are refused. A row claiming anything but Unsupported or Future over a summary that declares no MUST-level requirement, unless that summary declares itself non-normative or carries a manual-walk extraction sign-off. And a row PROMISING conformance -- Supported , alone or with a scope after it -- whose Proof cell says none of its gated MUST-level requirements is proven. A checklist nothing passes carries a support promise no better than an empty one, and the two escapes above do not reach it: each says the DOCUMENT imposes no MUST, which is a different question from whether Ze meets one. Partial is the honest row there, and it is not refused. Row presence needs no check any more. A row exists exactly where a summary declares a section, so an enrolled RFC with no row, a row naming an RFC with no summary, and two rows for one RFC are each unrepresentable rather than refused. Proof is the one derived cell in these tables. It restates that RFC's own coverage from rfc/requirements/<stem .md : how many MUST-level requirements the summary gates, then how many of them carry a test in BOTH polarities ( proven ), how many carry an annotation ( annotated , with partial scoped evidence shown as a subset), and how many carry neither -- one polarity only, or no test at all ( untested ). The three sum to the gated count. A summary gating no MUST-level requirement reads no gated MUST , and no cell an author writes changes any of it. Everything else in the table is editorial and no gate reads it. Status is a product-support judgement. It is neither the RFC's IETF category nor a derived value. Area is a hand-written label. Implemented coverage is source-anchored prose. One coverage limit is worth stating outright. A Remaining cell that spells its count in digits is not judged, and neither is one that puts words between the number and MUST. That is deliberate: the page uses a second convention where a number NEAR the word MUST is the not-applicable count.
